en: Preface to the Four Assemblies of Discourses by Chan Master Yuguan, the Venerable of Mount Jing.
Someone asked Lüan: "What is the greatest thing in the world? He replied: "Heaven and earth. [The questioner] asked:
"And what is the most luminous thing? He replied: "The sun and the moon. [The questioner] said: "In that case, the Buddha-dharma is also luminous and great."
[Question: "Is it equal to heaven, earth, the sun, and the moon? [Answer: "It is not so. [Question: "What is the meaning of this? [Answer:
"Heaven, earth, the sun, and the moon are that which dwell within form. Form is subject to arising and perishing and possesses limits and measures.
Even if there were ten billion Sumeru mountains, each containing ten billion suns and moons, ten billion sets of four continents, and so on up to the number of grains of sand in the Ganges River..."
All things have their limits; all things have their terminus. This is for no other reason than that they are confined within form.
If it were so with the Great Dharma of the Tathāgata, it would not be thus. Since it possesses neither physical form nor spatial location, who could bring it to completion?
Who could cause its destruction? I do not exist as the subsequent; who then could precede me? I do not exist as the lower; who then could stand above me? It is vast and indeterminate.
Ah, how sudden! How vast! How desolate! How subtle and wondrously pervasive! Its greatness has no exterior; its minuteness has no interior.
True Suchness is revealed alone; there is nothing that is not the Way. Thus it transcends the realm of heaven and earth and rises above the sun and moon.
Great to the point of being beyond representation—this is what is truly great. Brilliant to the point of being beyond...

This is clearly understood. Therefore, speaking in terms of sentient beings, from the four noble ones down to the six classes of ordinary beings, whether deluded or awakened, there is nothing within the Buddha-dharma that is not fully present.
Speaking in terms of insentient things, this includes water, fire, earth, and stone.
Whether among those grasses and trees, be they large or small, there is no place where the Buddha-dharma is not present.
The teachings of the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the canon cannot fully proclaim it; the eighty-four thousand gates of affliction cannot defile it. Alas!

Even if one were to take Mount Sumeru as a brush and the ocean of fragrant waters as ink, and write for unspeakably unspeakable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, could one ever fully extol the beauty of the Buddha-Dharma? Nevertheless, the Buddha-Dharma is inherently luminous and vast.
As for its spiritual brilliance within a person, though ten thousand kalpas may be distant, it does not depart from the present moment of thought. One—
If mindfulness is not established, one immediately ascends to the stage of enlightenment; this too depends solely upon one’s own self-exertion.

Although I, Lian, am not gifted, I have always delighted in discussing with those who study Buddhism. From the outset of my appreciation for the Way, I have never made distinctions based on the depth or shallowness of their realization;
I have seen much truth in this. Master Yuan’an, the abbot of Jingshan, received the Dharma from...
Yuan-sou Duanxin occupied four famous monasteries and propagated the Buddha-dharma, causing the ears of humans, devas, dragons, and ghosts to stand erect in reverence.
Monastics and laypeople followed him like clouds returning to their peaks.

His disciples, including Guantong and others, compiled his teachings into a written work and sent it through my friend Yongtang Bian Gong to request a preface. When I hung my lamp and read it thoroughly, its...
He untangles the human entanglements like a hawk shedding its tethering cord, soaring aloft to the clouds.

His skillful means for others are like a compassionate mother’s love for her child, looking back three times at every step. His total capacity and great function are like a great general facing battle;
as the banners and drums move, arrows and stones gather. Truly, he was a patriarch of his era, possessing both virtue and eloquence.
Is it not so? Nevertheless, within the Gate of Non-duality, not even a single dharma is established, much less words.

The reader should seek the meaning beyond the words of the Zen Master, so that both subject and object are forgotten, and even the forgetting of forgetting is forgotten; only then will one draw near to the Way.
Alas! The Buddha-dharma transcends heaven and earth and rises above the sun and moon; how could it be a trivial matter? People suffer only because they do not seek it.
Now, having praised it to the utmost, I have recorded this at the beginning of this collection, truly desiring to inspire reverence and faith in others.
To paint empty space—would one not be either foolish or deluded? I, Lian, am indeed unable to distance myself from such [delusion].
This is the responsibility [of the author]. On the twenty-first day of the second month in the eighth year of the Hongwu era,

this preface was composed by Song Lian of Jinhua, Imperial Academician and Attendant Lecturer at the Hanlin Academy, Grand Master of the Second Class with Rank Zhizhao, concurrently Compiler of the National History and Assistant to the Crown Prince for Good Counsel.

Volume One of the Recorded Sayings of Venerable Yuan’an.
The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master [Name], Compiled by his Disciples Guantong and Others at Longjiao Chan Temple in the Prefecture of Qingyuan during the First Year of the Zhi Zheng Era.

On the tenth day of the tenth month of the Renwu year of the Zhi Zheng era, the Master entered the temple in response to an invitation issued by the Imperial Commission for Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs (Xingxuanzhengyuan). Pointing [to the assembly]...
The Mountain Gate says: Peaks and ridges surge like the sea; towers and pavilions open like heaven. Here is Maitreya; here is no gate, and no Sudhana.
In the Patriarchs’ Hall: From patriarch to patriarch it is transmitted; from Buddha to Buddha they pass the hand. At midday they strike the third watch; facing south, one looks at the Big Dipper.
Entering the hall, he looked left and right and said, "There is no secret dharma to be transmitted here.
What is it that you all have come together to seek? He struck the meditation seat and rose.
Ascending the seat, he held up the incense and said: "This incense shares the same substance and root as heaven, earth, and the myriad things; it is most supreme and most great.

Its branches extend for a hundred generations, indestructible and unmixed; ever loftier and ever firmer. I reverently burn this in the precious incense burner, solely to pray for the ten-thousand-year reign of the present Emperor, His Majesty.
May the Emperor’s person be blessed with ten thousand years, ten thousand years, ten thousand times ten thousand years! We humbly pray that the mountains shall remain as firm as whetstones."

The rivers are like sashes; this is the foundation for ten thousand generations of great peace. Carriages share the same ruts and scripts share the same characters, expanding the transformative influence of non-action throughout the four seas.
Next, he holds up the incense and says: "The Buddhas of the three periods have no transmission; the patriarchs of successive generations have no transmission;
the elder monks of the world have no transmission. Today, Longjiao burns this incense in the burner as an offering."

The late Master Huiwen Zhengbian Furi Puzhao, the forty-eighth patriarch of Xingsheng Wanshou Chan Temple at Mount Jinshan in Hangzhou, Yuanzou Duan. Everyone, tell me: for what reason did he do this?
[He] struck the incense burner three times with the incense stick and then lit it. He then took his seat. Master Jixiang addressed the assembly:

After the striking of the staff was finished, a monk asked: "If Śākyamuni did not appear in the world and Bodhidharma did not come from the West, and the Buddha-dharma pervades all under heaven such that one's mouth remains closed when discussing the profound—why is it that you, Master, have appeared in the world today? Ultimately, what business is this? The Master said:
"A snake does not move without a head. The monk pressed further: "Since Śākyamuni did not appear in the world, why did he preach for forty-nine years?"

The Master said, "The Dharma has long since fallen into decay. Jin asked, "If Bodhidharma had not come from the West, what then? Yet, how could it be that Shaolin possesses the wondrous secret? The Master said, "In old age, one becomes possessed by demons.
Jin asked, "Whether the Buddha-dharma pervades the world or not, and whether the mouths that discourse on the profound are opened or not—these I do not ask.
But for the sake of the nation you have opened this hall; by what means can the imperial grace and the grace of the Buddha be repaid? The Master... [remained silent].
[The Master] said: "Those with eyes see; those with ears hear. The assembly prostrated. The Master then said: "The sun over the sea is lofty and bright;
the sea and sky are vast and wide. Peaks and ridges surge from the ocean; towers and pavilions open like heaven. Every single thing is the unsurpassed wondrous gate;
everywhere is the adamantine true essence. When the Buddhas appeared in the world, they passed down errors as truths. When the Patriarchs came from the West, they took mistakes as correct. One.
The Great Canon deceives the common folk; even monks with clear eyes cannot save themselves.

Yet, if one can be without mind toward affairs and without affairs within the mind, then one will see the wind of Yao sweeping vast and the sun of Shun shining bright; heaven will be clear and earth at peace, the people healthy and all things flourishing.

This mountain monk’s Way is thin and my person insignificant, yet I have received the distant command of the monastery to cross the seas and climb mountains across the three rivers and nine embankments.

Mount [Name] has opened the hall for this nation to proclaim the fundamental tenets. There is not a single thread or speck of deception toward you all, nor do you all harbor a single thread or speck of deception toward me, the mountain monk.
I hope that each of you will maintain sincerity and together reach a full mutual understanding.
Again, the case is cited. A monk asked Baizhang, "What is the extraordinary matter? Baizhang said, "Sitting alone on the Great Hero Peak.
The monk bowed, and Baizhang struck him. The Master said: "Great Baizhang understood only how to claim supremacy where there is no Buddha.
Suppose someone were to ask New Longjiao today, 'What is the extraordinary matter? I would simply answer him: 'All of you should [attain it]...'"
[He] became a Buddha. If others pay him homage, he further says to them: "Simply cultivate a heart of resolve, and you will certainly not be deceived.
He ascends the hall [and says]: "The mind itself is the Buddha; rabbits and horses have horns. Neither mind nor Buddha; oxen and sheep have no horns. Do you understand?"
The goddess Guṇakaraṇḍā and the woman Andhakārī—when a wise host refuses both, he descends from his seat.
Ascending the hall, the Master calls to the assembly; the assembly all look up at him. The Master says, "A hawk flies over Silla," and immediately descends from his seat.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the case: Linji said, "One person, for kalpas, remains on the road without leaving home;
another person, for kalpas, remains at home without leaving the road. Which of these two deserves to receive the offerings of devas and humans?
Linji’s insight was all-encompassing, yet he truly possessed only one eye. Yesterday, when I arrived in Changguo to visit various officials, I followed...
Going east and crossing to the west, going west and crossing to the east—restlessly hurrying from place to place, spending the entire day only on the road.
How, then, can one say that one does not leave one’s home? On this day of returning, one joins the palms at the mountain gate and burns incense within the Buddha Hall.
Passing through the Sangha hall and entering the kitchen or storehouse—these are all one's own dwelling. How, then, can one say that one does not leave the road?
Members of the monastic community simply require that things be discussed according to reality. If one does not discuss them according to reality, one is called a man of empty talk and deception;
how could such a person accept the offerings of devas and humans? Longjiao’s announcement in this manner is itself a minor deception.
"Furthermore, how do you speak a single phrase of plain reality? He then said: "From of old, I have never sung songs of deception;
I carry fire to burn the mountains and gather marsh snails. On the white tree-top, a fish-fan; on the rapids of a swift stream, a bird builds its nest. Good brother!
With his whisk, he struck the meditation seat and descended.
When Master Baotuo Guding ascended the hall for the morning service, a monk asked, “When Xinghua saw his fellow practitioner, he struck him down from the Dharma Hall;

what was the meaning of this? The Master said, “What common ground is there for conversation? The monk pressed further, “When Gaoting visited Deshan, he saw the flagpole across the river and immediately turned back;
how do you explain that? The Master said, “Ants do not eat iron. The monk pressed further, “Baotuo...”
"Venerable Da has come into the mountains today to visit me. How will you receive him? The Master said, "When we meet, there is naturally one who understands;
why must the pure breeze move heaven and earth? The monk bowed. The Master said, "A defeated general is not executed."
He then raised the case, saying: "Longya’s Way says: 'My elder brother, Yunju, attained the second phrase; I have attained the first phrase. The Master said: 'How great indeed is Longya!
He merely opens his mouth wide, unaware that his tongue drags upon the ground.

As for this mountain monk, I am currently honored by my Dharma brother, the Venerable of Bodha, who has condescended to visit this empty mountain with his carriage. I can only feel shame at my own neglect and lack of refinement."
"Making offerings—how could one dare to falsely communicate news? Guanyin Bodhisattva used money to buy a fried cake; when he let go of his hand, it was actually a steamed bun.
This is the second phrase. But what about the first phrase? [He] lets out a shout and descends from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Maitreya is truly Maitreya; he manifests a thousand, ten thousand, even a hundred million bodies.
From time to time he reveals himself to those of this age, yet those of this age all fail to recognize him.

The three hundred and sixty joints and eighty-four thousand pores of the Tathāgata Maitreya have all at once been cast into the laps of you all. I dare ask you: do you recognize them yet? If you do recognize them—"
It is attained. There is no Maitreya above in heaven; there is no Maitreya below in the earth. (He plants his staff upright.
At this moment, if you do not investigate the root source, you must simply wait for the future to question Maitreya.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "Speech is slander; silence is deception. Beyond speech and silence there is something further.
What is this thing that lies beyond? The Master said: "A monkey climbing a tree, its tail trailing over its head. The monk pressed on: "The path beyond is not transmitted by the thousand sages.
The path beyond is not realized by the thousand sages. Ultimately, what is it? The Master said: "Beyond."
The Way has always been right before one’s eyes. Thus it is said: "At the beginning of the winter solstice month, sell the quilt to buy the ox;

at the end of the winter solstice month, sell the ox to buy the quilt. With its three hundred and sixty-six days, including the intercalary month, it establishes the four seasons and completes the year.
Not even a single hair’s breadth can be shifted. Selling at a high price in the east and a low price in the west—where will you put your worn-out straw sandals after thirty years?
Entering the hall: Cold and heat alternate and press upon one another; today is the first day of the twelfth month. A drop of water freezes with every other drop; do not say it is merely cold.
Slowly, he descended from his seat.

Entering the hall, he raised the following case: Once, Attendant Guang said to Xuan Sha, "If you, my senior uncle, can realize Chan, I, your junior nephew, shall forge an iron boat and sail it into the sea.
After Xuan Sha took up residence there, he sent someone with a letter to inquire after Guang, asking, "Has the iron boat been forged?"

[The Master] said, "No. Guang remained silent. Later, Fenyang Zhao spoke on his behalf, saying: "One sees only the sharpness of the chisel’s tip; one does not see the squareness of the chisel’s handle. Xuangjue said:
"Xuan Sha is like a poor man brooding over an old debt. The Master said: "How great [the error] of Xuan Sha and Attendant Guang!
They have not yet forgotten self and other; they mutually expose their family's disgrace. For a thousand years hence, they will be subjected to scrutiny by others. Cui Ping [concludes]."
I do not imitate the ancients; everything here is simply as it always has been. Yesterday, the attendants from Lingyin and Tiantong came to visit me.

Once our greetings were concluded, we burned incense and shared tea. When the tea was finished, they were escorted back to their guest quarters. Naturally, host and guests found harmony in the Way, and the feelings between uncle and nephew were forgotten.
Today, as I ascend the hall, I briefly record this account. I humbly hope for your enlightened understanding.
The Buddha Ascends the Dharma Hall after Attaining Enlightenment. [The Master] cites Zhaozhou’s question to Nanquan: “What is the Way? Nanquan said, “The ordinary mind is the Way.
Zhaozhou asked, “Is it still necessary to direct one’s intention toward it? Nanquan said, “To intend to direct oneself toward it is already to deviate.
Zhaozhou said, “If one does not intend to do so, how can one know it is the Way? Nanquan said, “The Way belongs neither to knowing nor to not-knowing. To know is deluded awareness; not to know is...”
[This is] indeterminate. If one truly penetrates the Way beyond doubt, it is vast, open, and expansive like the great void;
how could one forcibly impose right and wrong? The Master said, "The transgressions of Old Teacher Wáng fill the heavens.

You have carelessly torn asunder and exhausted the unsurpassed Great Way that Śākyamuni Buddha attained through six years of bitter toil and myriad hardships on the Snowy Mountains. You deserve two [blows]."
Ten staffs. At that time, Zhaozhou’s eye-sight pierced through the four worlds. Let us set aside for a moment his being deceived face-to-face;
among those present today, is there anyone who can uproot the World-Honored One? If there is none, I, Longjiao, shall not remain idle in prolonging ignorance.
As one who is a distant descendant of the Bequeathed Teachings, I cannot help but extend a hand.
He brandished his staff, descended from the seat, and drove everyone away at once.
He then addressed the two senior monks, Zhen and Min: "The realm of true purity is a single void that has never existed;

yet, following conditions of defilement or purity, it manifests as the ten dharma realms. Throwing the fire, he said: "A Vajra molded from clay runs beneath the water; a Bodhisattva drawn with a brush."
Walking amidst the fire, he ascended the hall.
He cited Dongshan Yanzu’s address to the assembly, which said: "The Patriarch cannot describe it; the Buddha-eye cannot see it.

From the four directions, with a grandmotherly heart, I shall open a single thread for you. Having finished, he descended from the seat. The Master said: "If one were to cause frequent shedding of tears..."
"Even the vast blue sea must dry up.
He ascended the hall. A monk asked, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion?
The Master said, "The Stone Daring at the crossroads. As the monk prepared to ask again, the Master said, "You want another ladle of foul water! He then continued:
It was the third month; the season had reached Qingming. It was neither cold nor warm, half-shaded and half-sunny.

Fallen flowers and crying birds—call after call. Suddenly grasping his staff, he pierced through the nostrils of Xiangyan (He-kong), blinded the eyes of Bodhidharma, and, having worn out his straw sandals, walked barefoot away.
The fine mountains still remain upon the highest peak.
One day, while the Master was washing his hands, a monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master sprinkled water on him, whereupon the monk ran away. The Master called out, "Come here, come here! When the ancients were splashed with water, they would strike back and refuse to leave;
why did you run away? The monk then made a gesture of sprinkling water with his hand. The Master said, "You are interpreting this through intellectual reasoning. The monk then let out a shout.
The Master also shouted. The monk shouted back. The Master then struck him. The monk said, "Master, do not strike me in error.
The Master said, "You simply take this blow; I wish for these words to be put into practice."
Ascending the hall, he raised an ancient saying: "Form and sound are the lethal poison of non-arising; sensation and perception are the pitfall of the ultimate person. He further said:
"One must simply sleep amidst form and sound, and sit or lie down amidst form and sound. He then struck the whisk.
"Can it be called 'sound'? [He] raises the whisk. "Can it be called 'form'? "Apart from the mind and consciousness of discrimination, beyond words and phrases, bring forth a single phrase."
Ascending the hall on the Buddha’s Birthday, [the Master] remained silent for a long while and then said: "The Old Man Śākyamuni is born! The toads and earthworms together realize the Dharmakāya;
the pillar and the lantern together offer congratulations. Master Yunmen said, "If I had seen him at that time, I would have struck him dead with a single blow of my staff and fed him to the dogs;
those who ruin others are many, while those who help others are few. He struck his whisk and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall: "The water-mother and the shrimp; the *suoji* and the crab. The eyes are on top of the nose; the legs are beneath the belly. Descending from the seat.
When the Abbot Zangzhu Yuantaichu arrived, he ascended the hall and raised this case:
Venerable Ānanda asked Mahākāśyapa, "Aside from the golden robe transmitted by the World-Honored One, what else did he transmit? Kāśyapa called out, "Ānanda! Ānanda responded, "Yes? Kāśyapa said:
"Throw down the banner-pole in front of the gate! The Master said, "Ānanda asked thus, and Kāśyapa answered thus. Now tell me:
did the World-Honored One have anything to transmit at that time, or did he have nothing to transmit?

If you can apply a single eye here, then the entire Great Canon of five thousand and forty-eight volumes—whether provisional or ultimate, partial or complete, expedient or real, empty or existent—will not fail to be penetrated.
"From top to bottom. He picks up his staff and strikes once. "To give him noodles, one must use wheat from the Zhou lands; to sing the song, one must be a person from the Imperial Capital.
Entering the hall, he looks at the assembly and says: "The old monk has already set the whole tray out for you all. When hungry, one encounters..."
The King’s meal could not be eaten. Do not mistakenly think this is a matter of personal preference;

then he descended from his seat and ascended the hall. A monk asked, “When Mazu ascended the hall, Baizhang rolled up his mat. What was the meaning of this? The Master said, “One who has not undergone bitter toil does not know.
The monk pressed further, saying, “When the dragon’s sleeve is swept aside, the whole body is revealed; where the Elephant King walks, there is no room for foxes.”
"Traces. Have you attained resonance yet? The Master said, "From ten thousand *li* away, one gazes toward Yuezhou.
He then cited Dongshan’s words: "On Mount Wutai, clouds steam rice; before the steps of the Buddha Hall, it is a 'dog-urine sky'; atop the flagpole, a *zhuanzi* is being fried."
Three monkeys scatter coins at night. Shishuang said: "The wind blows through the stone mortar, vying in its roar; a clay-made Vajra runs beneath the water.
It tramples the moon over the sea, causing chaotic waves to rise; it startles the Earth Star, which invades the Southern Dipper.
Daowu said: "A three-faced cat treads upon the moon; a two-headed white ox grasps smoke in its paws. A crowned green hare stands—"
The Courtyard Cypress. A shell-shedding turtle flies up into the sky. Master Yong of Baoning said:
"Of these three verses, one is fit to serve as a teacher for Buddhas and patriarchs; one is fit to serve as a model for humans and devas; and one is fit to test the eyes of monks.
Let those with eyes discern them. The Master [Zhaozhou] said: "Baoning speaking thus is like a slave showing deference to a maid. Cui...
I spare no effort to break it open for you all. "After three transcriptions, the character *wu* becomes *ma*.

At the conclusion of the retreat, thanking the Chief Steward for providing the meal and the Librarian for holding the whisk, he ascended the hall. Biting through the iron-sour pastry, one finds all flavors complete;
performing the Great Canon’s teachings, a single phrase encompasses all. A three-legged donkey prances about on its hooves across ten thousand miles.

Not a blade of grass. [The Master] descended from his seat. Addressing the assembly on an autumn day: "I have taken up residence in this famous monastery on the edge of the sea; I am ashamed that my own path and merit do not match the illustrious legacy I inherit.

That the pillars of our school are left in such neglect is truly lamentable; though the Sage’s Virtue is like heaven, it is not easily repaid. You must hold the divine talisman behind your elbow; do not..."
Let trivial matters stain the mind. Last night, the golden wind blew down the leaves from the *wú* trees; from the north of the earth to the south of heaven, early autumn has arrived once more.
One day, as the Master entered the garden, he saw the head cook cutting melons. The Master asked, "How many heads of the Patriarchs have you harvested?
The cook replied, "Thirty. The Master said, "Which of these has blood beneath its skin? The cook replied, "Why do you, Reverend, trouble us so repeatedly?"
They were joking with one another. The Master said, "A good heart does not receive a good reward.

On the first day of the eighth month, he ascended the hall to request the appointment of the *jian-shou* (storekeeper) and to give thanks for the rain. He addressed the assembly, saying: "Today is the first day of the eighth month;

beyond the heavens, the clouds have cleared and the sun has risen. Last night, the Dragon King of Guanmen manifested great spiritual power, sending down a torrential rain that has completely [filled the fields]."

The great earth, its grasses, trees, and forests, as well as the rice, grain, beans, and millet, shall all receive nourishment and relief. Within Longjiao Monastery, everyone shall be employed in the supervision of harvests so that each person receives their due;
throughout the three hundred and sixty days of the year, it is guaranteed that there will be sufficient porridge and sufficient rice.
In Jiangnan and the two Zhe regions, where spring is cold and autumn is hot—[the Master] descends from his seat.
The posthumous letter of Master Shitang of Yuwang arrived; he was then entered into the Patriarchs’ Hall. Ascending the hall, [the Master said:

"For fifty-three years, I have been cleverly manipulating things until I became clumsy. I have trampled through empty space and walk barefoot; the myriad phenomena and the entire cosmos cannot stop laughing.
Great assembly, this is the final word of Master Shishi of Yuwang for the benefit of others. It is as clear as the bright sun and as vast as..."
The Great Void is fully endowed with both provisional and ultimate truth, as well as illumination and function; it possesses the complete mastery of seizing and releasing, killing and enlivening.

It can ferry the four modes of birth across and serve as a bridge and vessel for the nine realms of existence. A mosquito attempting to mount an iron ox finds no place to insert its beak. (He strikes the meditation staff.
If you see it here, there is not a single place where the compassionate countenance is not beheld, nor a single moment when the preaching of the Dharma is not heard. If, however, you have not yet...
After a short while, he descended from his seat. He requested that the assembly chant the scriptures to adorn their spiritual station. Where the incense smoke rose, all were free to gaze upon it.
When the Master arrived at Qianlan Zhuang, the assembly invited him to view the sea. The Master asked: "The great ocean does not harbor dead corpses; as for the fish..."
Water is life. Why then die in the midst of the sea? A substitute response says: "I am afraid it will rot. Another says:

"In the ocean of nature, where there is no wind, golden ripples surge of their own accord. [The question asks: "What is it like when suddenly encountering a whirlwind that topples the mountains? A substitute response says: "Profoundly still."
Upon returning to the monastery and while drinking tea, the Master said: "The deluded mind is the ocean; afflictions are the waves;
poison and harm are the evil dragons; worldly toil is the fish and turtles. These are all manifest in your daily activities—how can you avoid them?"

A monk picked up the tea pitcher and poured some tea before the Master, then walked away. The Master said, "That was truly a reckless pour. The monk looked back, and the Master immediately shouted and drove him out.
On the ninth day, he ascended the hall. A monk asked, “What is a guest among guests? The Master said, “You head toward Xiangxiang; I head toward Qin.
The monk pressed further, “What is a host among guests? The Master said, “Always on the road, yet never leaving home.
The monk pressed further, “What is a guest among hosts? The Master said, “Always at home, yet never leaving the road. The monk pressed further, “What about...”
“What is the Lord of Lords? The Master said, “Holding the Mo-ye sword crosswise, I issue the full command; throughout the realm of Great Peace, I slay the dull and obstinate.
The student asked, “The roles of host and guest have already been pointed out by the Master; as for the matter of the Ultimate Vehicle, what is it like?

To recognize it within the mental activities of sentient beings, if you wish to understand the meaning of its eternal abiding and non-transmigration, simply realize it at the point where the myriad things wither and fall.

yet, in truth, there are no sentient beings who attain liberation. Possessing all merits, these true merits are inconceivable.
It is not that Mañjuśrī would lightly reveal this; to whom could the gateway of perfect penetration be disclosed?
His protruding whiskers are like drifting clouds, his grooming is sparse; he carries a bottomless basket filled with crimson-vented carp. They are cheap in the east and precious in the west;
he need not worry that there is no market in the world. When the three-tiered waves rise high, the fish transform into dragons; yet the foolish man still scoops water from the wild pond.
What is heard is exhausted by hearing; what is emptied is extinguished by emptiness. Taking money to buy a sesame cake, one lets it go and finds it is but iron.
On precipices and sheer cliffs, the body of mastery is revealed. One may scoop up the moon from within the water, yet not a single dharma is used to bind people.
The skillful means of the Great Being are subtle and inconceivable; yet upon the tip of a single hair, he manifests a body of words and phrases.
All sentient beings within the Dharma-realm gaze upon, worship, and recite it; though the characteristics of speech are quiescent, they attain perfect penetration in their very presence.
I vow that in future ages, I shall practice without regressing and be fully endowed with wisdom and skillful means, just like Avalokiteśvara.
With eighty-four thousand arms in the *mudrā* posture, how could his compassionate rescue be limited to only four?
The Dharma-body is formless and does not fall into any numerical categories; yet, according to the minds of sentient beings, it manifests in all places. One is all, and all is one.
The moon reflects upon a thousand rivers; spring traverses ten thousand lands. I observe the Great Being: free from discriminative views, and even free from the absence of nature.
Day-face and Moon-face.

Impartially bestowing compassion, the Way reaches ultimate fairness; The six sense-faculties function interchangeably, all perfectly penetrating. As the tide turns back, a thousand waves merge upon the bay’s surface;

As spring permeates the flowering branches, ten thousand plants share in the same vitality. May all who are mired in ignorance behold the Sun of Wisdom; May all who suffer from feverish afflictions bathe in the pure breeze.
Great Compassion exhausts the realm of sentient beings to its voidness; Yet it remains as ever, the rising sun to the east of the sea (in praise of the Zen practitioner Nichidō).
The four inconceivables and two excellences—rabbit horns and tortoise hair threaded together on a single string. Who recognizes the true realm of the Universal Gate?
The heavens and sea are boundless, yet the moon is solitary and full.

Seated cross-legged, he lies supine like a blade of grass in an auspicious breeze; his jade-like face wafts fragrance as a smile unfolds its crimson hue. In a single thought, he universally observes immeasurable kalpas;
even the house cat and the white ox have realized perfect penetration.
The lotus-leaf boat is light, yet the sea of suffering is deep; sitting cross-legged, one listens thoroughly to the sound of the ocean tide.
Fish, dragons, shrimp, and crabs all attain Buddhahood, while countless ordinary people remain submerged on dry land.

The essence of the teaching in this Sahā world lies in sound and hearing; when hearing itself is dissolved by sound, the Way manifests its own majesty. It was not granted to Mañjuśrī alone to skillfully discern this:
the single path throughout the ten directions is the gate of Nirvāṇa.
The ponds and groves all expound the Dharma; the mountains, rivers, and lands together radiate light. The eye and sound, the ear and form, are constantly in samādhi;
how could it be that the mind’s hearing alone penetrates the ten directions?
The inconceivable and wondrous power of the layman Vimalakīrti’s supernatural penetrations is much like an empty fist used to deceive small children. I ask:

how does holding a date leaf on the point of a needle compare to containing Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed? When one contemplates the true mark of the body, how could there be much illness? To close the mouth in silence—
Self-deception! How laughable that the thirty thousand in the assembly on Vulture Peak, merely gazing at the wind, were all so listless they raised their white flags of surrender.
This is a sickness, yet it is not separate from the earth-element; nor is it apart from the earth-element. Alas, you old witless fellow! To open your mouth is already to fall into error.
Mañjuśrī failed to provide the correct testimony; thus he remains lying ill in the city of Vaiśālī to this day.

The Bagua Monk, a Honored One who manifests ten billion transformation bodies as a successor to the Buddhas, possesses within his sack a separate world of its own. He does not know how to preach the Dharma at the Dragon Flower Assembly.
I understand. But ultimately, how does one establish the gate of transformation?

Bodhidharma possessed the bearing of a dragon and a phoenix, a countenance like the sun and moon; yet he wandered aimlessly across the Yangtze River—what idle vexation was he seeking? Three or five [generations].
Back in the midst of poison; one cannot escape past debts. For eight or nine years facing the wall, practicing the heterodox Chan of silent illumination—tears have split my marrow and skin.
In a sudden turn of the body, I am unaware that my whole being has entered the wild weeds.

In the breast, cliffs and ridges rise ten thousand fathoms high; beneath the feet, waves and billows plunge ten thousand cubits deep. For what reason did he come from the West ten thousand miles away?
Only Master Liang should be his true知音 (zhīyīn—connoisseur of music/knowing one).

Wandering east and west until the skin of one's feet is worn through—how could there ever have been a separate transmission outside the teachings? Let it be that a single flower blooms into five petals;
a fine son never spends his father’s money.

The Arhat’s cultivation has not yet severed the poison of the rat; as one worthy of offerings, do not forget the kindness of the faithful laity. The dust and toil of the three realms are as deep as the sea;
with whom shall you join hands at the gate of Nirvana?
The Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai held an iron fly-whisk in his hand and let out a great lion’s roar: "The single mind is fundamentally empty and quiescent; even the three truths do not exist."
The lantern ascends the terrace along the wall; it startles the Dharmakāya hidden within the Northern Dipper.
The Sixth Patriarch—Zen practitioner from Zhangnan—requested a eulogy to certify that what is received is imperishable and that all phenomena are empty.
To touch upon a taboo in the current reign would be difficult to justify. Crossing the river on a single reed.
For nine years he faced the wall; before him was no Śākyamuni, and after him was no Maitreya. He split the skin and tore the marrow, greatly shaking the profound wind.
A thousand peaks reach the mountain, and ten thousand streams flow toward the source.
Bring forth your mind to rest; the mind is nowhere to be found. Having bowed three times and risen, stand in your place. Water does not wash water; gold is not bartered for gold.
The clouds part and the moon appears; the sun shines and heaven descends. Snow piled waist-deep; a sharp blade severs an arm.
Gazing up at his exemplary conduct, I am awakened to the impurity of my own form.

I bring my transgressions forward to repent, yet no transgression can be found. Realizing the wisdom of self-awakening, I extinguish delusive thoughts and afflictions; thus have I fully experienced all manner of hardships.
The fundamental limit remains unmoving; life hangs by a single thread. The lamp connects the three periods of time; this heart-seal of Vairocana is inscribed to instruct future generations.
The Yellow River flows in nine bends, yet its waters originate from Kunlun.
His side did not touch the mat for sixty years. Summoned three times by imperial decree, he did not rise. A thunderclap shook the nine heavens.
The Way was transmitted to the Lazy Monk; the robe was entrusted to a child. The moon descends upon the myriad waters; spring permeates the flower branches. All dharmas are entirely liberated.
The first phrase and the final stroke—how difficult it is for an old man to transmit the Way!
What difficulty is there in coming and going? Shedding this body to receive another, by the side of the turbid Hongjiang River, the marks and signs of perfection are complete.
Possessing great dhāraṇī and the thousand-jun capacity for the Great Dharma, this seven-year-old śrāmaṇera need not laboriously bring forth the matters concerning the mattock.
The twin peaks rise loftily; the green pines grow luxuriantly.

The Buddha-nature is fundamentally empty; how could there be north or south? A single phrase hitting the mark: the blue sky and the bright sun. There is no tree of Bodhi; the bright mirror is not a stand.
The Dharma was entrusted at the third watch; adding a cup after being drunk. A death-penalty plea with a living confession; when coming, there were no lips.
Planting flowers upon a stone; tying knots in the air.
When the monk Caizong was planting pines on Mount Poutou, he was lodging by the side of the Zhuogang River. The single thread of the Great Dharma hangs with nine weights.
The Tripod: Who can know the affairs of one’s coming and going?
Li Xizhi visited Yaoshan and said, "Clouds are in the blue sky;
water is in the pitcher. Only then did he realize that meeting a person is superior to hearing their name. Turning his body, he lost the way back he had come.
The Way: proceeding straight toward the deepest bottom of the sea.
The Boat Monk cast aside his oar and overturned his boat; the scaled dragon leaped once and passed beyond the blue mists. There is no need to plant the fishing pole again.
Bamboo. For a thousand ages, the waters of Zhujing flow backward.
Chan Master Yongming Jue took the mind as his school;
like a mirror reflecting a mirror, not a single speck of dust can remain, yet he universally responds to all capacities—like wind blowing over waves.
The radiance of the sun shines forth. If you wish to recognize the profound purport, it will blind your eyes. There is no dharma outside the mind; there are no forms within the mirror.
As I compose these verses of praise, I strike the void to produce a sound.
A prostrate tiger encounters a Chan master;

a village monk within Langzhan Monastery, an unruly son in the chamber of Mazu Daichi. Stealing the heart-bone and *śarīra* relics of the Tathāgata, he ascends Mount Sumeru upon a white ground of the Way.
Three Buddhas converse face-to-face; he speaks in his sleep with eyes wide open. As for him carrying a great fan at times—
At times he would enter the city to beg for money to purchase meat, yet he tamed fierce tigers until they were docile and showed no intent to harm people.
In guarding the precepts, spirits and deities would often kneel before him; in cherishing offerings, he did not even spare the water used to rinse his alms bowl.

These are all matters of his spiritual practice that are unfathomable—sometimes manifested outwardly while remaining secret within. How could those of inferior faculties and demonic nature possibly hope to fathom or deliberate upon them? One should...
The rulers of the Wu and Yue states showed him exceptional reverence; the Military Governor enlarged his residence for him and bestowed upon it the name Zhenji.
Thus he was known as the Pig-Headed Monk, the Great Master Pujue—one who ensured that the true tradition would never fall into decline.
Wandering to transform others, he rode a small tiger;
his true body, Pujue, was interred amidst five clouds. The winds of transformation rustle on as they did in antiquity. It is difficult to make the tiger cease its tendency to harm human intentions;
one simply requires that humans harbor no heart to harm the tiger.
Master Kaiyuan Fangya, the Zen Master:
The Great Square has no exterior; the Great Circle has no interior. Seated grandly upon his square couch, he brandishes his jade whisk horizontally.

He unleashed a great potential at the head of the Yangxian Creek and manifested a great function within the city of Helu. Mountains crumbled and rocks split asunder; it was like a flash of lightning or the roll of thunder.
His hands move freely across the surface; he possesses ample leisure.
Having pierced through the nostrils of every monk under heaven without moving his fundamental, spontaneous wisdom, he finds the clear river as pure as a silken ribbon—echoing Xie Hun’s famous lines.
Understanding the conditions of birth, he laughs at Wei Yingwu’s inscription for taking it merely as a description of the scene. He has overturned the gateway of stillness and illumination.
Overpowering and extinguishing the lineage of Miaoxi; though Baiqiao and Sengyou have depicted him, they have not captured his true likeness. "Nine times nine originally comes to eighty-two.
Ancient Tripod Monk, you who preside over the assembly, please bestow a eulogy upon this Compassionate One.
Iron Fenhua has occupied four seats of enlightenment; his eyes look down with contempt upon Buddhas and Patriarchs. Whether struck or touched by the bamboo staff, he acts with deliberate inversion.
He grasped it; lightning flashed and thunder rolled. Transversely and longitudinally he swallowed the thorny spikes whole. Gods loathed him and ghosts feared him.
Occupying Mount Lingxiao, he let out the lion’s roar for eleven years. His words filled the world, his Way filled the world, and his fame filled the world.
The cradle’s rope snaps, revealing the entire body; the great earth, mountains, and rivers leave not a square inch of soil behind.

*Recorded Sayings of Master Yuguan*, Volume Eight.
Verses compiled by the disciples Huijing and others,
sent to Dazhi Xuguting Jiangzhu (at that time at Wuliangshouyuan; forty practitioners were chanting the Avataṃsaka Sūtra in unison, with Xuguting presiding over the assembly).
I prostrate to the Great Dharma King of the Avataṃsaka. With the causal flowers of myriad practices, he manifests the fruit of wondrous virtue.

Shattering a single mote of dust, he brings forth this Great Sūtra; the power of his great compassion and Dharma is inconceivable. Contemplating all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm, one sees that the Tathāgata’s wisdom is entirely perfect and complete.
Yet through false imagination and attachment, they fall into delusion and inversion—like a vast sūtra scroll hidden within a single mote of dust. Such is the meaning of the various parables.
He extensively expounds and reveals them through the power of skillful means, vowing to cause both the small and the great to awaken and enter together into the Flower Treasury Ocean of Vairocana.
This Flower Treasury Ocean of Vairocana is boundless; its sublime merits are likewise immeasurable.
Its essence and function are fully manifested as the Great Vaipulya, yet in reality, no names or marks can be apprehended therein. Through eighty-four thousand dharma-gates, by...

Herein is established that which is conceptually differentiated: if there were even a single dharma, one would fall among ordinary beings; if there were not even ten thousand dharmas, one would lose the true realm.
The Dharma King, in accordance with the nature of reality, speaks with blazing intensity, yet from beginning to end has never uttered a single word.

The forty stages of the Mahāsattvas of the Dharmakāya—when the hearing and what is heard are both exhausted, there is truly nothing heard. Only when the teaching of quiescent extinction is heard can one thoroughly realize the true nature of the *Avataṃsaka*.
Within the Dharma-realm, one comes to know that exhalation and inhalation constantly turn like this great scripture. With different mouths yet a single voice, all recite it together;
the one is many, and the many are one. Jing Mountain’s verses are but mere praise; the power of the Great Compassionate One’s Dharma cannot be matched by words.
How excellent is the Samādhi of Immeasurable Life! Its golden and emerald adornments are peerlessly sublime. Āraṇya.
If phenomena are the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), then Tuṣita and Yāma are no different. The seven locations and nine assemblies are just as they are now;

in a single thought-moment, the three periods of time are entirely equal. The Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas of the future are one and the same Buddha; the bodies of the past and the bodies of the future are one and the same body.

I prostrate to the Dharma King, so rare in this world; like the Buddha’s appearance in the world for universal benefit, I pray that the Lord of the World may live for ten million years, and that the golden wheel and the wheel of Dharma may forever turn together.
May all those superior persons dwelling in the stages of abiding, practice, and penetration, as well as those of the mundane and supramundane worlds, join together in this Dharma assembly.
*Painting of the Arhats Crossing the Sea*. Written at the request of Ruhu, following the original rhyme, on the eighteen noble ones, those with training and those beyond training:
Their skills and wiles are not employed by the whole body; The alms bowl has a handle for scooping empty space.
With their staffs, they pick up Mount Hua and Mount Emei amidst the clouds. Naturally endowed with the three poisons, firm and unchanging— They often stand face-to-face, imposing and majestic.
Goes and chens—how could one recognize the white parasol by looking at them? Silent illumination—through this one realizes the "yellow-amber Chan.
Frequenting the palace of Sāgara, the great dragon beckons and the little dragon bows. Greedy only for the bright pearl from the dragon’s jaw, they do not realize their skirts and tunics are soaked.
Treading barefoot upon reeds as if on a mere footbridge, with hands folded they float cups, steadier than a vessel. O Wave God!
The sea goddess prepares offerings; rare and exquisite jewels vie with one another for beauty. Upon reaching this point, one must urgently ascend to the other shore.
The Master of the House calls out repeatedly. To play with the tide, one must yield to those who truly master the tide; how could one allow oneself to be called a mere "Arhat"?
Having realized that the fundamental nature of body and mind is empty, one transcends all sectarian schools whether following the waves or drifting with the current.

Even if one were to cut off one’s own shins, one would not encounter the legacy of Huangbo; who could recognize that single penetration of Gautama? By the bright daylight at the open window, the jade scrolls are unfurled;
with a single laugh, the spring breeze brings abundance to all life. When will I return to Tiantai and Yandang? Ten thousand ravines resound with the thunder of spring as the flying waterfalls roar.
The Song of the Blind Ox. Presented to Han Gongwang (Gongwang was a scholar-physician who, having suffered from eye disease in his middle years, called himself the "Blind Ox").
Seeing one's liver and gall through a wall, he calls himself the Blind Ox. I sing this song of the Blind Ox; the myriad phenomena laugh and nod their heads.
The blind ox—no one can recognize it. Since the beginning of vast eons, it has had no equal.
Moving freely among the diverse classes of beings, it hears sounds with its eyes and sees forms with its ears. The blind ox is a rarity in this world; a golden-maned lion is called a dog.
The grandfather’s fields and gardens are plowed to the best of one's strength. Strange sprouts and numinous herbs flourish in turn. Blind Ox—no afflictions!

Who cares about green, yellow, red, white, or black? With a single furrow, spring comes to the ridges after the fresh rain; with a few notes from the long flute, the dawn breaks over the riverside village.
Blind Ox—truly happy! From head to tail, heaven and earth are wide; his nostrils reach toward the sky, yet he does not cling [to anything].
Penetrating through, both birth-and-death and ignorance are completely transcended. Blind ox, blind ox, listen to my song! The six sense-faculties function interchangeably without partiality;
sentient beings see through with but a mere fraction of an inch. The ocean of lands of the great trichiliocosm is but an *amala* fruit.
Master Ying’an sent the farewell verse of Master Mitan; at Jiangshan, he was invited to harmonize with the verse on the "Dilapidated Man of Qizhou.
For the sake of the Dharma-gate, Wumen did not hesitate to show his affection for his son, failing to notice his own ugliness; the traces of those calligraphic remnants still remain.

Unfurling the scroll, the light scatters in disarray; it shakes the heavens and washes over the earth. One knows at once that on the day of this挥洒 (huishua—brushstrokes), the ink-well pool rained down like overturned basins.
With verses that are both poison and nectar, one severs the life-root at the critical moment. Mian Yun-chu once fell into a trap; do not blindly follow his example at Mount Zhongfu.
Next, the rhyme of the "Empty Room" (Kongshi): Presented to Attendant Jie of Central India.

In your family is the Patriarch, Old Man Xiashi; from the south of heaven to the north of earth, you have pursued the profound wind. Not only is your realization of the lineage thorough, but your mastery of exposition is likewise thorough.

You speak the Dharma freely, declaring that all phenomena are empty; looking down upon those who are mediocre and worldly, they are all but children. Yet this wondrous perfection does not involve emptiness.

Within the provisional and the middle, the second, third, fourth, and seventh are perhaps the same. In the realms of Śabdavajra, Kṣobhya, and Tuṣita, the great bell rings out with a deep resonance and the drums thunder.
A preeminent heir emerges from among a thousand men; he views all things with equanimity and casts his compassionate gaze. At the numinous stupa on Mount Mao, clouds of compassion enshroud it.
The lamp of Buddha-wisdom continues through Master Guangzhi; in this sagely era of the Tianli reign, we have personally encountered him. He is like the Buddha himself.
Supramundane merit and wisdom are full; the Central Indian Tamer, Hero among Gods and Men, whose compassionate vow to benefit beings knows no end.
He was accustomed to using glowing iron and molten copper; Xuan Sha’s fishing for fish took place upon a solitary raft. Shi Gong’s lifelong vocation was his single bow alone.

Wielding great banners and drums like a supreme commander, how joyful is the heart of Lǎn’ān! I love you for entering the inner chamber with a rosy countenance; your浩然 (hàoqì) spirit spans the void like a rainbow.
Having fully mastered the teachings of China and abroad, your reputation is lofty. Do not be in such a hurry regarding your plans to return to Fúsāng.
The Great Dharma, heavy as a thousand-jin weight, rests upon your person; as for me, an old man, my hearing and sight are like those of the blind and deaf.
To the Chan practitioner Ding of Qimín:

When the autumn evening falls upon the monastic groves, the ancestral lineage hangs by a single thread like a strand of silk. To study the Buddha, one must clarify the mind; to practice Chan, one must realize one's nature.
The emptiness of mind is itself empty; the head is straight and the tail is straight as well. Stone Gong bent and broke his single bow, bringing forth Xuan Sha’s three kinds of illness.
This was shown to Chan practitioner Yong of Yanzhou.
If one can skillfully employ the mind, one will obtain supreme and wondrous merit; this is the time-honored maxim of the ancient sages.

It values that the person remains undeluded. Unfurling the seven-foot single mat, straightening the spine of cast iron, standing as if at the edge of a ten-thousand-fathom abyss, with a wrist possessing more than a thousand-jun of strength—before is no Śākyamuni, behind is no Maitreya. Last night, by the Tóngjiāng River...
The waters flow upstream; the fishing platform submerges and rots the stone of Yan Guang.
Next, following the rhyme of Zhongzhu, I send this to Yuan, the Abbot, while also addressing Master Chushi:

with a brush-array sweeping across the field, in the style of Yuanhe, he has written out that first move prior to the time of Wei-yin, wherein provisional and ultimate truths are clearly manifest, and principle and phenomena are in harmony.
Complete. The Buddhas and Patriarchs let their heroic strength slacken slightly; on level ground, they overturn the Thousand-Year Rock.
Radiant, brilliant, and even more majestic—this Old Man fully employs a mechanism beyond the ordinary, not like the common "black bean" teaching.

Master of the Repository, your dharma-sound is like the spring sun; moreover, your years are still in full vigor. Yet the tradition of Shaoshi has fallen into bitter desolation; you must exert yourself.
The remaining light is raised by his power; how could Huangbo have struck Linji in isolation? Yunmen’s matter was already settled by his master.

In the Hall of Many Jade Banners, we joyfully meet one another; the ten-li wide lake opens like a mirror. I am deeply ashamed that my own negligence and indolence must daily respond to others, stirring my body and mind into a tangled skein.
This old public case left unfinished by my late teacher—upon whom can I rely for its critical judgment?
I send these words to the Elder Chushi of Qin River: An old steed, galloping with vigor, should shed its blood and sweat.
As Mishouze returns to Jiahe, I also extend my greetings to the elders of Nantang, Tianning, Santai, Xingsheng, Zisheng, and Guyushan.
The黄梅 (Huángméi) rains have ceased, and the river sky is cool. A fragrant breeze blows from the south, and the days are long. I am unwilling to dwell in this quiet room at an ancient temple;
instead, I recall that Bingzhou is my true hometown. As I depart, you extend a paper and ask for a long verse. Let your hand flow freely without begrudging the lack of fine phrases.
This is precisely the time when the Dharma is weak and Māra is strong; the collapsing framework of Jibei must be lifted up. Now, throughout the four seas...

O Nantang! You have cleared away the chronic ailments of the Buddhas and Patriarchs like a physician treating the *gao-huang* (the incurable spot behind the heart). You are like the morning star appearing beside the waning moon; your pure radiance shines brilliantly across one quarter of the heavens.

I further admire the foremost monastery of Nanhu, where amidst the scattered rubble and debris, the Dharma is proclaimed with blazing intensity. The jade palaces and crystal halls appear upon the tip of a single hair, requiring not the slightest exertion of the wrist.

The dragon pool below is straight and bottomless; its vastness— (Note: The source text appears to be a fragmentary verse or inscription, likely from a Chan Buddhist context. The final character "浩" [hào] suggests the sentence continues with a description of vastness or majesty.)
The vast source of the Pine Spring has its origins and its tributaries; it is not like the common quicksilver or silver of medicinal alchemy.

It truly becomes a single drop of lion’s milk, where the mists and vapors of Hongzhu connect with the cool streams of Shuangxi. The elder blows the *xun* while the younger blows the *chi*; they unfurl the Buddha’s hand and stretch out the donkey’s hoof.
Their transverse and vertical wondrous functions are all fully manifested. With a single laugh, the Elder Vimalakīrti of three lifetimes hears that his entire body has entered [the Way].
Weeds overgrown. Having thoroughly penetrated the ancient masters of all quarters, you who seize the market and bypass the ranks are no ordinary person.
Before the Drunken Plum Pavilion, it is best to return; wherever you encounter anyone, trouble them with my regards. That the same wind blows across a thousand miles need not be discussed;
I know well that the Head Seat possesses many virtues.
Master Yingzang returned to Huain. The sun and moon wax and wane;
the lunar mansions and stars are arrayed and spread out. The rivers flow and pour forth; the mountain crags are towering and steep. These are revealed everywhere, point by point.
Every single thing is fully revealed. You have personally entered my chamber; though you have a mouth, it can only be hung high upon the wall.
Originally there is not a single dharma to be transmitted; the plucking of the flower and the smile became a mere mess. One breath turns the entire Great Canon;
the myriad phenomena and the vast cosmos all fall prostrate. It reaches the point where the waters of the Long River flow backward, and atop Mount Lingxiao, the sun shines brightly.
With sincere courtesy, you request words of praise from my sleeve; this is much like stirring ashes in search of a spring. Within the breast of a man of integrity lies heaven and earth;
the yellow leaves used to stop a child’s crying are not true gold coins.
Following the rhyme of the Western Chamber: Presented to the Abbot Ding.
For forty-nine years, the Tathāgata preached; The partial and the complete, the half and the full—none were lacking. Yet from beginning to end, not a single word was ever spoken.
Without cause, he has once again leaked the secure gate. A man of the Way maintains his resolve to travel for study; With valor and diligence, he illuminates the path.
The Banner of Wisdom: With the hand of faith, he overturns the ocean of the Flower Treasury; from the treetops, pairs of fish are startled into flight.

This causes even empty space to break into laughter, while the ten thousand phenomena stand in reverent attendance. Furthermore, who cares about the "True Person of No Rank" who constantly enters and exits through the gateway of the face?
Have you not seen? Old Zhaozhou’s eyes had no tendons; when the Great King arrived, he did not rise. When asked, "All dharmas return to One;
where does the One return? he instead said, "In Qingzhou, I made a robe of cotton cloth that weighed seven *jin*."

In the same rhyme, a gift to the Dharma Master Fuzang, the Unsurpassed Honored One of Two Feet: Fortune is sufficient, and wisdom is likewise sufficient. The gates of the Dharma are widely opened to deliver all living beings. Six times six remains thirty-six.
The Great Canon’s teachings are a tangled skein; If one examines them closely, they are, in truth, a total error. Jiazhou.
The great elephant suddenly turns over; the iron ox of Shanzhou has its horns broken off. You are of the noble lineage of Longhe—why labor in vain to seek elsewhere?
Five thousand scrolls are but paper with sores upon them; the ten sages and three worthies are but tally-sticks for a privy.
There is no fundamental basis; there is simply a reason for its coming. Heishan only knew how to beat the drum; Xuefeng was solely devoted to rolling the ball.
Enough, enough! Springtime is like wine; spring rain is like oil. Letting go in accordance with conditions, wandering freely as things take their course.
Everyone says the flowers of Luoyang are like brocade, yet they do not know that spring resides at the tips of the willow branches.
Following the rhyme of the Western Chamber: Presented to Chan Master Zhencang.
One who studies the Way is like a fragrant elephant; cutting through the current to cross the river is truly heroic.
A colt tramples everyone underfoot; a single shout deafens even Baizhang. From antiquity to the present, not a single hair’s breadth has been lost. Exert yourself in practicing the ancient Way.
To decline such toil: with a single breath, one turns the entire Great Canon of Teachings. To dissolve it, the Golden Northern Dipper stands high;
who would say that the Patriarch’s taboo name should not be lightly touched? The descendants of the Five Heinous Offenses have no face to show. What is the Buddha? Three catties of flax.
Directly beneath, the three essentials are divided to form six.

He showed Chan Master Chang of Fujian that [this Dharma] cannot be covered by heaven nor carried by earth; how could it be something that an ordinary person is able to shoulder? Even the great and small patriarchs [could not do so].

Whenever questioned, they merely say, "I do not know; I do not understand. They cross oceans and climb mountains, traveling thousands of miles east and west searching for it, yet it is neither this nor that.
At the very moment of putting on clothes and eating food, and at the place of defecating and urinating, it is like a shadow following a form.

Seeking others is not as good as seeking oneself. Have you not seen how Xuansha Shibei, before he had even left the mountain, possessed such great spirit that he kicked through his mother’s birth-footprint, his brilliance illuminating the entire world for a hundred generations?
In the same rhyme. Presented to Chan Master Zong of Xiubei, who gazes south at the Northern Dipper: Reeds bloom amidst the flames; one phrase brings salvation to the Sanxuan of the Jibei school.
When brought forth, it stops the mouths of the patch-robed monks. The Great Canon and the Lesser Canon—both gathered in and both released. At the bottom of the vast ocean, all is submerged.

Amidst the crimson dust of the horse, atop the peak of Mount Sumeru, he beats white waves that surge to the heavens. This weary man of Jingshan, lacking any skill or artifice, offers but a short song;

he strikes the void to produce a sound. He envies the Dragon River for its ability to ensnare dragons and strike down phoenixes; with hair from a tortoise’s head, he weaves a net three thousand fathoms long.
An Inscription for Chan Master Bao-tuo Chun (Disciple of the Great Sage of Sizhou):

The Avalokiteśvara atop Mount Baotuo is the Great Sage within the city of Sizhou. His wondrous spiritual powers and marvelous functions are exercised with total freedom; everywhere he acts as if it were springtime in the midst of winter. When Deshan saw someone enter the gate, he struck him immediately;
when Linji saw someone enter the gate, he shouted at him. Those who understand this say: [...]* *Note: The original text appears to conclude with an ellipsis indicating the end of the inscription.*
His joyful relinquishment, compassion, and kindness—those who do not know him call him the ordinary Meng Ba. This man of the Way has traveled throughout the world for consultation and study;

he plucked the pearl and entered straight to the bottom of the vast ocean. Once the verdant green before his eyes is clearly distinguished, the shallow and deep beneath his feet are naturally understood.
Showing the patriarchal core of Master Xiuzang: unable to distinguish the golden sand, tying knots in empty space, planting flowers upon stone.

The entire Great Canon is met with a single word—a pillar supporting earth and heaven, a tethering stake for a donkey. Suddenly snapping the golden lock, the celestial qilin is set free; he casually brushes it aside.
The moon has fallen to the edge of heaven. If you understand, all things are of one family; if you do not understand, there are a thousand differences and ten thousand distinctions.
Nanda the Demon eats thorns upon his head; Vajra-pāda bleeds from beneath his feet.
The Head Seat departs for Japan. Following the rhyme:
"Is it right? Is it wrong? Neither right nor wrong. With a seven-foot black staff slung over his shoulder, the Head Seat has always possessed his own strengths.
Before his feet had even crossed the threshold, I already knew him. There is no need to speak of mind or nature; why must one strike the gavel upon the elephant-hide mat?

Greeting with bows, burning incense, and drinking tea—clear as a mirror reflecting a mirror. Last night, Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra gave rise to views of Buddha and views of Dharma, and were banished to the two Iron Ring Mountains.
Forget the dream of ascending Tuṣita; the sword hangs between the brows, and he turns over in his tracks.
Leaning against the land of Fusang, the eighteen returns from the South Sea and Persia;
Zen Master En, wishing to travel the quarters,
rolls up his sleeves and draws out a long verse, without further engaging in deliberation— clearly I present this for you.

The mountains of Min and Yue stretch for ten thousand layers; the waters of the Yangtze and Huai flow for a thousand li. Whether moving forward or backward, wherever the staff-tip points, it is all one’s own ground.
Where there is a Buddha, one must not dwell—yet what harm is there in lingering for a moment? Where there is no Buddha, one must pass quickly by—yet this is precisely the time to linger and play.
When meeting rice, eat rice; when meeting tea, drink tea. When it is time to go, go; when it is time to stop, stop.
"Tread through the straw sandals and return early; do not wait until the autumn wind shakes the trees in the courtyard.
To show Pure Mind Chan Master:
"If the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure. In every land and every atom, there is the Great Perfect Mirror. If the mind is empty, all phenomena are empty. Yesterday...
At night on the Southern Mountain, a tiger bites a large beast. In Zen practice, one seeks only to clarify the mind-ground. Shenkang stood in the snow and once severed his arm;
when the mind cannot be found, that is the pacification of the mind. Master Bodhidharma had no fundamental basis: "I have no mind at all."
What use are all dharmas? It is better to return home with the mind having attained emptiness as the first rank. Ten thousand *li* of northern wind blows the *bi-fu* reed-pipes.
[This is] a response in the same rhyme. To the Chan practitioner Shou of Donglin:
studying the Way is like employing troops; skillful fighting is not as good as skillful defense. One who knows how to speak does so without using the tongue; thus one understands.
The practice of the fist is not the hand itself; why trouble yourself by casting aside Donglin to seek out an old man at Xilu?

Since you have entered directly with a single blade, I shall immediately seize you with my dark staff. Having recovered your whole body from the tip of the staff, I do not yet permit you to open your mouth wide.

The Chan practitioner Chengxin, having purified his realization and perfected the study of the Way, saw that the myriad dharmas are but mind and consciousness. At every turn he beheld Śākyamuni; in every place he encountered Maitreya.
A true student of the Way, a genuine practitioner, a great man: Śākyamuni and Maitreya are his servants.
He dries up the four great oceans with a single breath from his nostrils; he hangs Mount Sumeru upside down by his eyelashes.

Wandering freely at will through the celestial realms, roaming at ease according to conditions in the imperial capital—how could Master Zhigong be a mere idle monk? And what of Bodhidharma, that old, coarse barbarian? One manifests as ten.
Regarding the "Avalokiteśvara Facing Two Directions": he asked them, "Which one is the front? One said, "Vast and empty, there is no sage.

[The Master replied,] "How can the primary truth (paramārtha-satya) be 'non-existent'? You must transcend it; do not allow yourself to be smeared with delusion. National Teacher Jingjue’s functional application was exceptional.
Pearls are scattered within a purple silk curtain.

It reveals the uselessness of that which is used, yet uses that which is useless. It is non-action for the sake of action; it is non-doing for the sake of doing. It flows vibrantly and rolls on; it is luminous and vast. Yet, it resolutely seeks me out as nothing at all.
To employ them as empty words is like adding feet to a painted snake; it is the uselessness of the old man who knows whether he knows or not.
To employ while being without employment is non-action (*wuwei*); red dust flies from the bottom of the great ocean.

To employ while being without employment is non-activity (*wuzuo*); an eight-cornered millstone grows in the void. To employ while being without employment is that even "non" is non-existent; a gnat swallows Mount Sumeru. Thus it is.
To proceed in such a manner, I do not yet dare grant my approval; there is another matter for deliberation. To flaunt one's verbal cleverness is useless, O Elder—how could it be right?
It would be better to let him use it as he sees fit; do not seek for flaws in a solid lump of cast iron. Act as you must act.
When hunger comes, eat; when cold, wear clothes. If you wish to act, then act. When spring arrives, flowers bloom; in autumn, leaves fall.

You must know that to practice while clinging to the Dharma is precisely like binding oneself without a rope. Have you not seen what the Patriarch said: "When the Great Function manifests before one..."
There is no fixed rule. An arrow is placed upon a mulberry branch; sap flows from a willow tree. Its wondrous function is as vast as the sands of the Ganges—how could it have an end?
Furthermore, one does not see that the Great Master Fu once said: "Empty-handed, I grasp a hoe; walking, I ride a water buffalo."
In the latter part of the night, I play with the bright moon by the Twin Streams; look at the bridge over the flowing water—it does not flow.
The new Head Seat has returned to his mountain dwelling in Jingxi.
Following the rhyme of Yinxin: "The Mahayana vessel was born in the Divine Land; ice withered and snow aged through many autumns. The azure clarity before the eyes of the Hu monk—"
Consciousness! You have traveled far and wide in vain upon this land of True Dan. A single word is easy to utter but difficult to retract; for nine years he faced the wall by the side of Mount Song.
His misfortune reached those who stood in snow waist-deep. Seeking the mind and finding it not, one is as frantic as drilling wood.

A seeker of the Way came from Jiangdong asking about the Way; ten thousand monks followed him like clouds from Longhe. The sword-gas between his brows brushed against the Ox and Dipper constellations. Meeting him just now—

How excellent is the spirit of this school! Five leaves and one flower, each opening in full bloom. Bodhidharma never transmitted anything to Huike; had he not seen the old Master Yaoshan of those days?
Doing nothing at all, he sat in meditative repose. O seekers of the Way, you should return to the chambers of pine and stone;
there, you may walk and sit with ease and freedom. If someone asks about the matter of the "Western Arrival," [Yaoshan] showed his fist, as large as an alms bowl.
Venerable Xueyan’s Song of Herding the Ox. Chan Practitioner Qing requested a response to Xueyan’s “Herding the Ox”:
The mechanism was not kept secret; From east to west across the stream, his tracks were revealed.
This drew forth an ignorant, blind fellow, Who spent all day wandering aimlessly in search. How does this compare to Changqing, who herded for thirty years? Such is the power of taming.
This has a profound provenance. Sometimes fully released, sometimes fully gathered; moving freely in all directions without restraint.
With a casual flick of the whip, the old plow and harrow are cast aside with a single "sha" sound. Let them be scorched by the sun and blown by the wind;
when hungry, eat; when cold, wear clothes. From head to tail, heaven and earth are vast; the nostrils point toward the sky, the two eyes are alive. At the three-pronged fork—
At the crossroads, the evening sun glows crimson. The wine banners flutter wildly against the clear sky. A short flute is blown from west to east.
Falling petals and drifting cotton fluff fill the spring air with misty haze.
In the same rhyme: Sent to the Abbot Deng:
Birth and Buddha are fundamentally equal. To travel among teachers, one must see one's nature. The body of sentient beings has no marks; The crown of all Buddhas cannot be seen.
Radiant light pervades the dust motes of all lands, shimmering and reflecting one another. This treasury is neither a treasury nor not a treasury; it is neither mind nor object.
Whether diminished by a little or increased by much, it never falls into deficiency or surplus. The cricket chirps as the autumn night draws long; the bird sings as the spring day stretches on.

Brilliantly clear, it utterly transcends concealment; distinct and vivid, it is free from partiality or correctness. Subject and object realize true emptiness; whether in accord or in opposition, they entrust themselves to the mandate of Heaven.
The ocean of Dharma is vast and boundless; in every step, one may freely swim and play. How lamentable is the man of Yajñadatta, who, in his delusion, vainly pursues the reflection of his own head.
Zhen, the Abbot of the Tripitaka Collection, returns to Wu. He also sends this letter to his Dharma brother Wan-shou while on his travels.
Following the rhyme of Quan-shi: The *Vairocana* treasury pierces through the seven and eight apertures; It does not abide within the ten mysteries or the six characteristics.

More than five thousand scrolls have been erroneously transmitted; Discourses on nature and mind are all but echoes and shadows. The plucking of the flower and the smile held no underlying intent; Cold and warmth are known by oneself, like a fish [in water].
Drinking water. Two, three, four, seven—these are but empty transmissions. "The Superior Man (Shang Daren), Qiu Yiji. In my youth, I lived upon Mount Huiri;
there, I trod firmly over many elephants and dragons. You, being young, excel among the talented and eminent; you have diligently explored this Way and followed me in my travels.
Now that I am old and decrepit, I am no longer what I was of old. I rejoice that you, at Longhe, have come to knock at the door of Quanshi. Quanshi.
The Great Dharma King of today possesses for people nothing more than a whisk of tortoise hair. With eyes upon the crown of his head, he distinguishes the heterodox from the orthodox;
block your ears and cease listening to empty clamor. This child of the five rebellious acts has extinguished the ancestral wind; Buddhas, patriarchs, and celestial demons alike follow his commands.
The Northern Mountains share my heart’s melody; there is no need for you to trouble yourself sending a single sheet of white paper.
Tell him that I shall surely return to the south sooner or later, so that we may look upon one another while roasting yellow tubers over a fire of dung.
The Zen practitioner Yūzen invited the Tripitaka and returned to Japan.

Following the verse on Sudhana’s southern pilgrimage, he met his first friend; he grasped the nostrils but lost the mouth. With a snap of the fingers, the gates of the multi-storied pavilion were flung open.
Shaking throughout, shaking everywhere; roaring throughout, roaring everywhere. Ekō En comes from Fusang, crossing the whale-waves directly without hindrance.
Winding along, he followed the wind for five days until he reached the Middle Kingdom. He joyfully beheld the myriad peaks of the sea-mountains, towering and azure.
Having procured five thousand and forty-eight fascicles of the Tripiṭaka scriptures, how could he have feared the length of the mountains or the distance of the waters?

Tomorrow morning he shall part from me and return to the East; you must lightly turn the prow of the boat. You must know that the Great Dharma is fundamentally without transmission. Forests and waters...
The bird constantly proclaims it; before the Stone City Mountain, it turns its head back again. The Buddha-sun shines upon the southeast heavens.
To Vimala: A gift to Chan Master Manzang. Following the original rhyme:
Phenomenal existence is not different from true emptiness; the illusory does not depart from the real. Why then, in this empty room, do you hang up "emptiness"? This...
The room has neither front nor back; it is as vast as empty space. If one were to abandon the solid and immediately grasp the void, all six openings would become obstructed.
When the room is wide, the oceans of boundless lands are all contained within; when the room is narrow, even a hair’s breadth of extraneous object finds no place to rest.
Whether wide or narrow, real or void—cut this off right before you. There is no need for calculation or deliberation: the ten ages of past and present are but one.
When mindfulness is present before you, there is no separation at all. This room is neither empty nor existent; it depends entirely on the person to maintain it well.
In the midst of ordinary harmony, everything is overturned; even a sneeze becomes the lion’s roar.
