The Zen practitioner from Yuan returns to the East; within the Great Tang there is no Buddha-dharma. Do not leave even a trace of the character "Yuan" in your breast. Traveling on foot to visit various quarters, you shall surely know for yourself.
To cure an illness, one does not need medicine carried by a donkey. Old Dharmatrata, that hairy barbarian, came from the West and committed a great error. Every person—
The nostrils point toward the heavens; each and every one has eyes shaped like triangles. Directly pointing to the human mind, the mind is fundamentally empty;

seeing one's nature is to become a Buddha, for a Buddha is simply awakening. When spring arrives, the flowers bloom of themselves; when autumn comes, the leaves fall again. Tread through your straw sandals and go back home;
across ten thousand li of sea and sky, a solitary falcon soars.

Shishanju demonstrated that Chief Seat Chijian maintained secret practice and profound silent illumination. Holding fast, he reached the limit; letting go, he was spontaneous. He could truly roll up or unfurl [the world], establishing a heaven and earth beyond the square;
transverse and vertical, he hung the sun and moon within the realm. What need is there to speak of "a sword hanging between the eyebrows"?
Blood splatters against the Brahma Heaven. Have you not seen how, after a single glimpse of Master Ma, Daiman grasped his nostrils and lost his mouth?
He went straight into a thousand peaks and ten thousand peaks; who would be willing to hide their body within the Big Dipper?
And have you not seen when the weary old man Longshan lived in his hermitage? The mud ox that entered the sea left no further trace; one knows not what year it is in this dusty world, but—
Seeing the sun rise in the east, the one dwelling in the hermitage recognizes the master within the hut. The wildcat climbs upside down upon the Bodhi tree;
it does not hinder the hundred birds from coming to offer flowers. Let the vegetable leaves drift away with the current as they please.
The Ballad of Dongting: A Parting Gift for Jiaze Tang.
Dwelling between East Dongting and West Dongting upon the Water-Moon Mountain, one gazes down upon the thirty-six thousand qing of Lake Tai, where the white waves stretch out in vast majesty.
Above, seventy-one or seventy-two wondrous peaks pierce the sky, their elegant hues as azure as the void; golden spires are arrayed like stars, shining brightly against the Milky Way.
The path to the forest abode is deep and remote, leading to the vast blue sea. Lu Gong’s stone screen remains majestic, as if possessing a living presence;

one still imagines his thunderous commands summoning wind and lightning. Furthermore, one admires how Cishou delighted in secluded seclusion; there, trees, forests, and waterbirds together perform the subtle Dharma, expounding upon the True Vehicle.
Shining through antiquity and illuminating the present, these two elders are praised; looking up and down, who else shares this Way? Within the moonlight upon the water, a rare talent is found;
though the stage for the dance be small, one may still perform with skill. With a pure body and a broad, long tongue, he sits firmly amidst the lakes and mountains, preaching with fervent intensity.
Where the waters and sky meet boundlessly, the moon is solitary and full; all moon-reflections in the water are subsumed within that single moon. Yangqi has just settled here.
The four walls are empty; with bitter toil he tills the fields to earn his daily meal. Fengxue, though dwelling alone, is as majestic as a thousand-fold assembly.

His lofty style from a hundred generations past stirs the vast void. He restores the true regulations of former masters and sweeps away the dusty traces of later followers. He plants a single blade of grass.

The manifestation of jade towers and crystal palaces does not yet fully embody the total transmission. Spreading a net across the heavens, he strikes the scarlet-scaled fish leaping through the waves without expending further effort;
his fragrant influence flows as a celestial omen, producing a noble scion. Linji was no mere "white-handed thief."
The Ancient Mirror. Presented to Zen Practitioner Ming.

Before the primordial chaos was divided and before the world was established, there was a single radiance of spiritual brilliance—profoundly still and eternally tranquil. It silently reflects the myriad phenomena.
It penetrates and illuminates the ten voids, interpenetrating and encompassing all without deficiency or excess.

Whether it be "the Hu comes" or "the Han comes," whether it be the "face of the sun" or the "face of the moon"—at the moment of seeing seeing, that seeing is not seeing; this you call the ancient mirror. You should investigate its essential meaning, for it shines through antiquity and soars through the present.
Illuminating heaven and reflecting the earth—this is the profound source. To the Zen practitioner Ding, I present these words:
The true source is profoundly still; stir it and it becomes turbid, yet when illuminated through tranquility, it is like a mirror without a trace. Suddenly, the waves of emotion arise.

Suddenly, the waves of consciousness flow and turn through the three realms, manifesting in a thousand manners and ten thousand forms. I exhort you to the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*):
abandon the five turbidities together, so that every particle is pure and every world-system is tranquil and perfect. (The above consists entirely of verses in mixed long and short meters.)
The Recorded Sayings of Master Yuyan, Volume Eight.
The Recorded Sayings of Master Yuyan, Volume Nine:
Verses and Eulogies.
Compiled and read by the disciples Hūvī and others:
The Dharma-realm of the Avataṃsaka is vast and boundless; Like jade turning and pearls revolving, it fills the eyes before one. Ultimately, one must transcend the nature itself.

The ocean of the profound is still stained by the defilements of the mind’s field; though not departing from this very place, it encompasses the three virtues. To explain through various indirect methods is to manifest the ten mysteries.
How shameful that the honored father, Vairocana, deceives his children with a mere raised empty fist of partial understanding!
Reading the sixty thousand words of the *Lotus Sūtra*, the Supreme Vehicle, I face a cold window as incense smoke rises in curling patterns. Boundless parables are like honey on the edge of a blade;

The great causal conditions are like ice within a fire. A single snap of the fingers need not hinder the opening of the jeweled stupa; Who can understand how to continue the practice of self-immolation?
Zhendeng: He traversed and counted three thousand scrolls of ink; with a single phrase, he completely transcended the power of memory and intellect.

Reading the *Śūraṅgama*, he contemplated the Buddha’s Crown-Śūraṅgama Samādhi; from the Golden Mouth, the flowing pearls were each perfectly round. Great Samādhi is never apart from cultivation for ten thousand [aeons].

Practice! First, through the secret cause, sever the three conditions. Within the tip of a hair, lands appear beyond the reach of thought; in the locus of the eye, one perceives sound, transcending both correctness and partiality.
If you can truly explore the ocean of teachings with empty hands, know that once the fish is caught, the trap must be forgotten.
Reading the Great Chapter of the *Laṅkāvatāra*, its profound and secret meaning is deep; the "yellow leaves" used to stop a child's crying are superior even to true gold.

To fully realize that the mark of self is originally no-self, one directly reaches the source of the mind—how could there be a mind? The horns of a hare or the hair of a tortoise cannot serve as metaphors; let the waves of emotion and the surges of consciousness run their course.
Floating and sinking—cast aside both the hundred negations and the four propositions. Even gnats and ants can understand the appreciation of sound.

Reading the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*, the Great Perfect Enlightenment Sea is vast and even deeper; who would believe that the true source can be sought nearby? The three contemplations are clear and bright, marking what is beyond [conceptualization].
The moon: the six sense-objects are pure, the ore is primordial gold. I pity the Tamer for his excessive eloquence; he did not permit Mañjuśrī alone to appreciate the true sound.
Opening this scroll merely seeks to shield my aging eyes; I have no intention of seeking realization through fixed schedules.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was transcribed in blood by fifty-three men who came through bloody battles; the misty waters of a hundred cities were all turned to gore.

The pavilions of Vairocana surged like crimson clouds, and the mountains and rivers of the Indra-net opened as red banners. From the tips of ten fingers, the lion’s roar resounded; upon the point of a single needle, the elephant [trampled].
The King returns; the presence or absence of his power is difficult to conceive. A pungent wind immediately pervades the nine realms.

This copy of the Lotus Sutra, written in ink by the lay devotee Wang Yuanji of Songling, was produced by a husband and wife who together upheld the Wondrous Dharma Flower. It makes the Empty Space laugh to tears, and the Prabhūtaratna Stupa.

The pagoda; startled, it overturns the white ox-cart on the open ground. Though worldly conditions have not yet ended, what hindrance could there be? Having personally ascended the jewel-treasure site, one will certainly not err.
Each and every blue lotus flower appears within the finest detail; the remaining strength in his wrist is truly worthy of praise.

The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra with embroidered characters—this numinous text of Prajñā has long been my karmic affinity. In leisurely embroidery, the work is perfected with joy. Silver hooks and iron strokes are arranged in their respective rows;
jade thread and golden needles reveal the wondrous mystery. That a rabbit conceives a fetus is but a superfluous teaching; that a clam holds the bright moon is not... [the true reality].
True Exegesis: The adamantine true essence is majestically revealed; embroidery upon brocade, the five colors are brilliant.
The two masters Qin and Yin together transcribed the *Avataṃsaka*;
from the tip of a single hair, they manifested the Great *Avataṃsaka*. Its names, phrases, and phonetic forms are sublime and wondrous, unfolding together with jeweled nets and cloud-palaces.

It is said: "The realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) encompasses all down to a single hair; sentient beings together enter the treasury of Vairocana. In the Brahma-garden, twin blue lotuses (utpala) bloom;
upon opening the scroll, there is not a trace of written characters. Sudhana ran in vain through the hundred cities to the south."
Keeper of the Treasury, your term completed, you return to Wu;

from ancient times to the present, when has there ever been awakening or delusion? At Nanping, I lazily blow upon the monk’s robe-hair. The mountains are green, the clouds are white—the treasury of radiant light.
The magpies chirp and the crows caw—these are but minor verses of elegance. Ten li of level lake, autumnal and serene; on the road back to the Three Wu regions, the millet ripens.
Farewell, farewell. Do not regret that there is nothing left to entrust you at parting; it is merely to once again settle the eyes upon the brows.
Written by the Monk-Yuanpan, by imperial decree, while returning north after offering incense at Yuhuang Baota (Potalaka), in response to the rhyme of Master Xuechuang as a gift.
Master Sengsiji of the West River, a lion among monks, descended from afar with celestial incense and returned across the sea. His *śarīra* emit precious light in five colors;
the Great Being of Laṅkā dances upon the three terraces. Atop the solitary peak he meets Maitreya; at the tips of the hundred grasses he recognizes Sudhana.
May the Sage Ruler live ten million years in non-action; the Buddha-dharma in the South has not yet been entirely reduced to ashes.
Reply to the Secretary’s Letter. Furthermore, I send this note to Master Lin Li.
Zhuofeng, you were already able to scatter earth; now you can even scatter sand. A difficult elder brother and a difficult younger brother—what joy for those of the same clan!

A man-eating lion with its full set of teeth and claws; a Han-lu hound chasing clods of earth while trailing its tail. Waiting under the moon for a hare at a stump is in vain; striking the grass with the staff is intended to catch the hare.
A startled snake; when the collapsing纲 (gāng) is vigorously restored, observe the efficacy of the task. What prevents one from planting beans and yet obtaining rice and hemp?
Treasure Store Master returns to Wujiang;

the Dharma King’s Great Treasure is hidden within the Secret Form Mountain. To meet face-to-face and seize the opportunity—this is difficult to perceive. The draft of the paper robe is entirely [filled with this].

Mistaken! To let the firewood fall aimlessly is utterly groundless. A divine steed at birth possesses the will for ten thousand *li*; a colorful phoenix soars to the heavens with its five-colored plumage.
The guiding ropes of the Shaoshi lineage are only now beginning to loosen; you shall not yet be permitted to lie high and idle by the banks of the Qujiang.
No words—since beginning to end, not a single character has been spoken. To open one’s mouth is clearly to fall into duality and three. Nine years at Shaoshi resulted in leakage;
a single silence at Vaiśālī revealed the subtle flaws. The records of Chan explanations are but paper full of sores; the nets of the Teachings are but layers of falcons.
Stinking Shirts. The broad and long tongue cuts off the sound of the stream; The spring wind and flying swallows chatter on their own.
In the same rhyme, answering my Dharma-brother Mengtang:
North and south, amidst the clamor of war and strife, Brothers separated as if by another life. On the vermilion mountains across the vast ocean, you hold your banquet.
Seated. Amidst the ashes of kalpas at the Double Path, I walk alone; it merely adds a bundle of bamboo strips to the weight around my waist.
As before, the eyebrows still stretch across the eyes. Fortunately, the ancestral home remains intact; thus, one may strike the third watch even at midday.
The Way shown is identical to that of the common people;
how could the Great Way ever have difference or sameness? As soon as discrimination arises, one deviates from the fundamental principle. Majestically and alone it is revealed beyond sounds and dust;
clearly and distinctly it always dwells within movement and function. The bright mirror is not a stand, for its light illuminates itself; Bodhi has no tree, for its essence is...
Yuan-k'ung. Far away, the dragon soars as men return to distant lands; through the ages, who can truly revitalize the ancestral wind?
Answering his Dharma brother Pu-chi Yuan-shu’s sharp wit, he brushes past the traces of Mu-chou.
As the ceremonial banners and canopies are raised, they gaze upward toward the Five Peaks; the flower-gatha sent from afar still lingers in the spring.

Early morning. I open my window of ivy to enjoy the snow just beginning to melt. The towers and pavilions rise abruptly above the Wu River; tiles and rubble lie scattered across the paths and valleys.
Do not disdain my tardiness in composing this reply; though we brothers are a thousand miles apart, our spirit is originally one.
The Master Miaozang traveled to various quarters;
his realization was pure, perfect, and uniquely wondrous—his son understood this deeply. Why need one trouble oneself with seeking elsewhere? Liangsu saw no end to his encounters with Magu;
Deshan fell into a trap at Longtan. Like a falcon piercing the clouds, breaking through the sun, and soaring beyond the heavens, he gallops alone across the void, dripping with sweat.
The crimson steed; from within the sleeves, the *maṇi* jewel emits strange radiance, illuminating the hundred cities southward across misty waters.

A single drop from the inexhaustible source flows forth from the void of kalpas; its gentle current never ceasing, it flows afar to pay homage to the sovereign. Who can fathom the origin of this vast and enduring flow?

Its power waxes and wanes, entirely transcending the workings of creation. Though it floods the heavens and drenches the sun, its essence is never extinguished; how can its branching and flowing ever be exhausted?
Throughout the ten thousand ages, the monastic forests are equally nourished; together we rejoice that the true lineage of Caoxi remains unobstructed.
In the same rhyme: Sending off Attendant Jun from Japan to enter Min Province.
Three calls and three shouts, as if in a state of shock; the bowels and entrails are shaken loose and poured out for you. The Master’s functional pivot is intimate and direct;
the attendant’s majestic deportment is perfected in old age. A *zhālù* staff hangs from the tip of a branch in China; it floats within the eye of a gnat.
Penglai and Yingzhou: Listening to the autumn rain atop Tianfeng Pavilion, one must know that what fills the ears is not sound.
In response to Su Changling, Editor-in-Chief. While ill, I requested tea:

"The Elder Vimalakīrti of the Eastern Land and the Western Heaven has not been seen for autumn, yet the dust of thirst does not arise. I constantly recall taking my meal at the Fragrant Accumulation (Gandhavyūha) Hall."
The kingdom has not yet had leisure to inquire after his illness in the city of Vaiśālī; his profound discourse directly seeks to transcend all verbal expression.
How could there be any idle sentiment for peaceful sleep? Zhaozhou said, "Go and drink tea"—how many people's eyes did he blindfold?
In the same rhyme, I respectfully respond to Imperial Preceptor Zhang Tü-xuan’s request for a stele inscription for my ancestral master, Venerable Shanquan.
The literary brilliance of the Elder Minister shines forth; he takes the four great elements as his meditation seat, and his pen is accustomed to inscribing the *Vajracchedikā*.

The eyes, hands, and face are grandly opened upon the great field of quiescence. From the whale-ocean, you have again taken the trouble to send your poem from afar; at the dragon-pool, I deeply rejoice that we may forget our worldly selves through the Way.
Standing tall upon the western ridge is the Patriarch’s stupa; I await your composition as you descend from the imperial capital.
Next, following the rhyme of Master Nantang Liaohan, I shake my sleeves at the First Peak of Central Wu: Nantang stands towering, his lofty wind chilling;

He causes the true regulations of Vulture Peak to be restored, Far surpassing the unobstructed flow of the Songyuan lineage. The morning star shines brilliantly across the heavens, Like a wild crane soaring freely and beyond compare.
The cage: there are times of ease, yet no place to rest. Fengdian and Hanshan Shi are exactly the same.
[In the same rhyme: To the Chan practitioner Jian:
the physical form of the banana tree is fundamentally not solid; the roots of birth and death are deep, entangled by suffering. With a single stroke, cut it in two.
Section. Why need one inquire about the Way or practice Chan? In the sand pot, every meal is leek soup and rice; in the stone cauldron, there is always the smoke of cypress seeds.
When the three periods and the ten directions are all cut off at once, who knows who comes after and who comes before?

In response to the "Heavenly Chapter," my younger dharma-brother Louluo, the Wise One, lectures on Tiantai. His eloquence reaches the heights of Master Lu’s mirror-stands; every dharma is without discrepancy, for waves are but water.
In moment-to-moment non-abiding, fire turns to ash. With the power of correct exposition, he refutes heterodox views, exhausting all the challenges that have come from the south.
Coming from the North: the descendants of the Buddha-sun flourish with exceptional brilliance; the iron flowers bloom once more upon the treetops.
On the anniversary of the passing of the Master’s Patriarch, Wenyuan Weng of Shanguan, I am moved by the scene and compose these seven verses.
Today, the twenty-fourth day of the fifth month, this aged, decrepit monk has just manifested through transformational birth; within the rank of Buddhas and patriarchs, there is no abiding place.
Adorned, one wanders aimlessly upon the path of humans and devas. Towering and steep, the mechanism of the stone is still formidable; precipitous, the Dragon Rock speaks of Great Practice.
If you wish to know the ultimate meaning of the Skillful Means, when the sun is at its zenith, it strikes the third watch.
The fragrant breeze makes the days in the courtyard seem longer; throughout the entire realm, all is manifest and unrevealed. Now, young pines vie with one another to break ground from the earth;

in the old garden, new bamboo has already overgrown the wall. One knows for certain that the flying squirrel is no other thing; suddenly, hearing the singing cicada, one is reminded of the setting sun.
Sixty-six years have passed once more; there is nothing of birth or extinction to be reckoned or measured.
The demon of illness assails me as I grow old; I lie high upon my square couch within this small room. This physical body of the four elements is fundamentally illusory;

the karmic obstructions of many lifetimes are originally empty. Whether in the jeweled palaces of the Flower Pond or the Avīci Hell, amidst the conflagrations of Mounts of Swords or the Tuṣita Heaven, I roam at will through heavens and earth.
Opening my window, I vainly attempt to draw in the profound breeze of the Dharma.
Cherries and *lú-jú* are planted around the eaves; a small square pond was opened by my own hand. Tandi does not forget his written vows;
Huangmei once again mounts the wheel of salvation. Many bodies wait for their turn across the dust-like lands; how could the whole being refuse to nourish the holy embryo?
With meager merit, I dwell on this mountain head already white-haired; how can I repay your profound kindness even with a drop of water?

The halls and buildings, vast and grand, have been renewed from old to new. Every inch and foot of length is wondrously woven into design. One knows the labor and skill in every bamboo head and wooden shaving;
one recognizes the bitter toil in every pillar and lantern. From Xiangji, the spring is led to Bai Zhang; from the tiered towers, the gaze extends beyond a *yojana*.
Yet, how I pity the places where one sits, lies, and walks—every single thing fully manifests the pure *dharmakāya*.

Out of love for this cluster of ten-mu gardens, where the red blossoms have faded and green shade extends; walking daily with my staff has truly become a source of delight, and gathering wild vegetables from time to time costs no money.
Linji planted pine trees by personally tilling the earth; Yangshan sowed millet by burning his own fields.
To whom can this ancestral livelihood be entrusted? Standing alone beneath the southern eaves, I am filled with desolation.
The affection of licking her calf seems as deep as the sea; who would have known it was the grandmotherly heart of Huangbo?

The essence of nectar, cream, and curd are all of one flavor; hairpins, bracelets, vases, and trays are all the same gold. With a snap of the fingers, one completely transcends the Dharma, Reward, and Transformation bodies; with a turn of the body, one cuts off past, present, and future.
Amidst the fragrant breeze within the high hall and white walls, beholding the portrait once more, my thoughts cannot be restrained.
Seeing off the Elder Xiang and the Elder Qian, who reside at Miaoxiang Fashi in Xuanchou;
following the rhyme of Old Man Xi of Wānlíng’s ancestral home: In the morning, I joyfully see off my grandsons on their journey. May you cherish one another, elder brother and younger brother.

I pray that you practice for the sake of the Dharma, not for fame. Though the clouds and mountains lie a thousand li away, they remain vivid before my eyes. The single thread of the ancestral lineage is even more so.
Touching my heart: The papaya tree scorched by the sun and buffeted by the wind cannot be fully depicted, nor can it be drawn.
In the same rhyme, I respond to the letter sent from Master Zhaoming Caiwuxue, Abbot of the Thousand-Year Temple beneath Mount Jinfeng.
Amidst the Hall of Horizontal Verdancy, I am but an old man; day and night, the source of my mind remains ever limpid.
Ji: His icy frost-like discipline is uniquely fresh and pure. Amitābha is his present companion who forgets his own form; Maitreya will be his future guest within the tent.
May he share the same birth-year as Zhaozhou; I send this tea, wrapped simply, as a token of the spring before the rains.
The Yi and Zang masters completed their term of office and returned to Chengtian. Next, Chan Master Gangzhong Yunyi recited one great collection of the Buddhist canon in a single breath.
Turning his head toward his native land, he saw it was the realm of Fuchai; startling the multitude, he joyfully beheld a man of heroic spirit.

Cease presenting the "perfect circle" (yuanxiang) to those who are already veteran masters. With the vital energy arising from his palms, he confronts birds, tigers, and rhinoceroses; with the true eye atop his head, he discerns all.
Dragon and serpent; in the late autumn of the forest, one beholds the towering stumps. Throughout the entire world, the five-petaled flower blooms.
(In the same rhyme: Sent to Chan Master Yuan of Kaihua:

Tired of gazing upon the verdant hues of the tree of merit, you find that your native mountains are truly superior to distant lands. Mulberry and hemp spread across the plains and marshes, intermingling with fragrant scents.

The path leads to a jeweled monastery where golden and azure pavilions stand tall; in the small study, snow melts by the hearth as clouds fill half the couch. With new verses strung like flowers, a thousand lines flow daily;
in the depths of spring, are the four elements at ease? To the Buddhas and patriarchs, we rely on their scales to lift and lower us.
I have retired to Haichun to receive further instruction. Xie Xiang has come to visit me at my mountain hut.

Following his rhyme, I write this upon dispersing the assembly and returning to rest; I am ashamed that I am but a withered old man. To guide disciples and propagate the Way, I leave it to those in all quarters. For a hundred years I have dwelt in illusion, relying on the foothills of the clouds.

At midnight, as I recall the transmission of the robe at Duidang, I pick wild bamboo shoots and ferns when the season calls—a taste truly exquisite. The cedar and pine trees I planted by hand have already grown tall.
Accomplishing Practice. In the spring breeze, we have toiled together on this short staff; Our entire livelihood has been for the sake of raising it up.
[Response in the same rhyme: To Master Jiān of Línghyìn, Yìngshì:
Following conditions, there is nothing one can do; Speaking the Dharma in autumn, joy is free from demons. Striking empty space with the gavel of Mount Sumeru.
The drum beats; the Prajñā-boat crosses the waves of the sea of suffering. At the head of Shizi Hill, the tide comes early; on Plum Blossom Island, the moonlight is abundant.
The river’s flow never exhausts its profound meaning; alone it permits the Wu accent to sing the Chu songs.

Setting out early from Yuhang, I am moved by the vast regulations of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, which provide a standard and guide. I feel ashamed to frequent the gates of nobility when there is nothing there of worth;

instead, I gaze upon the five peaks shrouded in mist under the third-watch moon, and the thousand crags and myriad valleys frozen with ice. Let my heart and its traces remain like withered wood; why must my name be inscribed upon the records?
The Transmission of the Lamp: Awakening Heaven makes the void not empty; in profound stillness, one watches the Sun of Wisdom rise.
(In response to the original rhyme. Answering my Dharma brother Yuzhong:
At Baohua, white daybreak rains upon the empty mountains. Your verse, filling the paper, honors me from afar. Suddenly, I perceive the auspicious vapors of the Five Peaks.
Gathering [the assembly], he causes the ancient style of a thousand years ago to return. His sweeping and brilliant calligraphy employs the "iron hook and lock" technique;
his refined and majestic prose is like jade pendants and rings. Incense is burned and drums are beaten to invite all to behold it; a radiant expression of joy moves his withered countenance.
Entrusting this to Tianning Bai’an: I have heard that Nanhu is the foremost mountain. Dragons and elephants mingle with the ranks of officials. The east end is expensive, the west end is cheap;
when one comes empty-handed, one returns with bare hands. A single stroke from the crown of his head is like a flash of lightning; the samādhi of his speech is like—
A Linked Verse: An iron ship descending into the sea—do not rashly set forth. This old uncle’s discourse on Chan is but a forced smile.
In response to Dharma Master Boyuan of Donggao, two verses:
The Venerable of Donggao dwells hidden among the outskirts and hamlets; His humble *tusu* hut is his Tuṣita abode. He carves cypress wood to serve as incense for his morning recitations.

The Dharma: Unrolling the curtain to welcome the moonlit night, I unspool the scrolls; in the village garden, the borders are ripe after the autumn frost, and moss grows upon the flower paths following the lingering rain.
When mind and objects are both forgotten and all illusions extinguished, where else could one seek the *tathatā*?

Summoned to the imperial presence, his audience was a source of great honor; his lofty eloquence and vast wisdom delighted the hearts of all. One wondrous truth cannot be exhausted in ninety days of discourse;
amidst a thousand distinctions and myriad differences, he realizes non-arising (*anutpāda*). Among the Great Beings (*mahāsattva*) of Central Wu, he is ranked among the three most eminent;
among the high monks of the Imperial Capital, he is the foremost. His Way is weighty.
The Sage Son of Heaven of the Golden Wheel wanders with ease upon the crown of Vairocana’s head.
Following the original rhyme, I send this to my Dharma brother Xingzhong:

Your banner and canopy have traveled east and now halt at the northern mountains. Together we tread upon the mottled traces of moss in our green sandals. It has been ten years since we last saw one another amidst the dust and wind.
Separated. How many times have you returned with empty hopes for news? To prop up jade chopsticks within the mouth of a fierce tiger; to untie a golden ring from the chin of a lion.
When the banner-pole has fallen, who shall raise it up again? Who envies the one who, grasping a flower, alone broke into a smile?
In the same rhyme, sent to Master Deyan: Old and decrepit, Longtan received the virtue of Deshan;
Where the paper lamp was extinguished, one peers through a tube at its speckled traces. How can this compare to the wondrous vital mechanism born at Dongta?

With all his might, he pulls back the orthodox pulse of the Western Cessation (India) and restores it. The brilliantly blooming flowers are truly noble and wealthy; The limpid sea of nature is of itself vast and pure.
Whirling and circling. Amidst crimson cliffs and emerald peaks within the autumn light, when shall I break into a laugh and reveal my withered face?
Again, responding in the same rhyme to my Dharma brother Fuyong:

In vain have I pursued hollow fame across the Five Mountains; Rushing about, I have only earned the graying of my hair. The lineage’s纲 (guiding principles) lie prostrate on the ground; I am ashamed to be of no help.

Supplement: The seasons flow on in haste and do not return; this floating world of a hundred years is like a snake clinging to its burrow. A weary life in the three realms is like an ant circling in a loop.
The equality of the holy and the common is difficult to regulate; looking upon my own meager talent, I am filled with shame.
Reply to my elder brother, the Dharma-teacher Fangyay, regarding the two verses previously sent.

The weight of religious talent depends on its application; as we brothers grow old, our mutual concern increases all the more. In vain do we labor with the teaching of lands and the teaching of dust, taking every sound of the wind for the sound of rain.
I have heard that Fayun once withdrew from the world with courage; who else has attained such lofty leisure as you, O Jue?
The heavens are clear. I hope that those who travel the final path to join the ranks of the mystics will all be made to return home and cease their questioning of the journey.
In the late autumn, the forests lie empty upon the earth; this small hermitage is not like others.

Holding up the single phrase alone on the Three Rivers, amidst ten thousand distinctions and a thousand differences, there is but one illumination. The Boatman’s pure breeze comes from Jiaqiao; Master Mazu finds his kin among the heterodox.
Master Pang: From afar I know where the black-robed and white-robed alike gather; when night falls, they burn tall red wax torches.
In Lamentation for Master Chushi, Three Verses:
I am a grandson of the old, decrepit Xi, who repeatedly received the Dharma from you in your advanced years.
How kind! Wearing hemp sandals, he ascends directly to the Golden Hall;
with his iron staff, he occasionally knocks at the gates of Baixia. Amidst the sea of affliction, he lets fall rain and dew; upon the back of empty space, he establishes heaven and earth.
When the song of non-arising is sung to its conclusion by the autumn wind, even the white ox and the stray cat find their spirits severed.
The Holy Sovereign questioned ghosts and spirits with ease; a single silence in the moment weighed as much as ten thousand pounds.
Under the direct decree of the Golden Gate, the cremation revealed the pure Dharma-body in its entirety. On level ground, the Buddhas of the three ages were startled and overturned;

in an ordinary act, the people of the entire city were blinded. How immeasurable is the power of his great compassion! Where the flowers bloom upon a withered tree, there is a spring of a different kind.
Seated cross-legged upon a simple couch, we converse with laughter; his final verse, written by his own hand, is like a string of pearls. The wooden horse neighs at night—a sign of certain departure;

the sun rises in the West, a phenomenon without precedent since antiquity. His emanations far exceed those dwelling in celestial realms; let him not forget to propagate the Dharma in the imperial capital.
Our white-haired brothers grow old in vain; the stupa pole has fallen and now requires someone to support it.
In the same rhyme: A congratulatory poem for Chan Master Xiangyuan upon his relocation to the Ten-Thousand-Fathom Dragon Gate at Jingwu.

The dragon gate of ten thousand fathoms at Jingwu has welcomed his triumphant return; fish leap from the mountain head as the dust of the world settles. Having penetrated the vital mechanism of life, he has transcended all conditioned existence;

his wondrous function, free and unrestrained, reveals the myriad subtleties. His reputation as a master is weighty throughout the monastic groves of the four seas; his character is as clear as the three high offices.
The stars are sparse. My grandfather’s stupa can only sustain me for old age; I intend to prepare a coarse cotton robe to ward off the cold.
Using this rhyme, I send it to Chan Master Quanshi of Tianjie, who has been summoned to lead ten thousand monks at the ancestral altar.
On the Dragon River, the flower-rain falls in profusion each day. Returning from court, the dawn light breaks upon the yellow [robes].
The Way: Concentration gives rise to numinous light that encircles the Purple Microcosm. Shell-palaces and pearl-temples exist within the heavens;
the Dharma King’s Chan is rarely seen even among the eyes of the great. When shall I once knock upon the chamber of Vaiśālī, smiling as I take up his golden-red *kṣauma* robes?
Reply to my Dharma brother Xingzhong of Mount Huqiu: He came to visit, and suddenly news arrived that the old fellow from Yunyan had returned.
Autumn winds blow across the waters as a single sail flies; An iron phoenix soars toward the heavens, breaking free from its golden net. A horned tiger emerges from the emerald peaks.
Few in ancient or modern times have the courage to withdraw from the swift current; We look upon each other, brothers with white hair.
Rare indeed! May you share the thousand-year lifespan of Baozhang; at the peak of Wujing, I shall once again shake out my robe. Following the original rhyme:
The livelihood of Tianxi Tang and Taining is utterly without a single needle;
he maintains the direct pointing tradition of our school with great vigor, skillfully reducing what is excessive and supplementing what is deficient.

Excellent! Transverse and vertical, all are perfectly suited. A divine mechanism flashing like lightning, complete with the powers of life and death; wondrous words flowing like pearls, brilliant and manifold.
By the side of Jiulihu Lake, he spreads the Dharma-gift; let him freely cause his disciples to propagate and uphold it far and wide.
Attendant Hui returned to the Rumen attendant’s quarters after having attained Zen.
With horns upon his head, he is a tiger; with wings sprouted, he flies. He makes Master Sheng laugh until he topples the nodding stone.

He shall surely transmit the bare-shouldered robe of the Patriarch Long. In assessing his merit, how could it merely surpass the stage of Dry Wisdom? To observe him proclaiming the Way, one must look to Xian.
Great Capacity. Do not harbor idle sentiments for an old uncle; the long river is well-suited for the iron boat to return home.
(In the same rhyme, responding to the letter sent by Youqi Zong. Two Poems:
Magnificent prose like five-colored clouds bestowed from Heaven; the weary traveler by the Dragon River reflects on his scattered thoughts. One night at Yongjia, then at Caoxi.

In the chamber, the wise cultivate both the gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Though people differ across the ages of past and present, both the teachings and Chan alike look up to the Honored Dharma King.
He opens wide the Buddha’s hand and stretches out the donkey’s feet, leaving all quarters at liberty to engage in idle debate.

A multitude of eminent talents stand out like a wind-borne banner; their eyes gaze upon the clouds and sky while they lie amidst the weeds. It was not permitted for one who knows his heart to push open the gate and rise;
would he have been willing to descend the mountain merely because of a message? The great, cool tree originally had no seed; the sacred sprout of Prajñā has long possessed its roots.
Competing in praise, the talent of Chu must be employed by Jin; he alone shall be the preeminent leader among the assembly of monks.
In the same rhyme: Lamenting the Venerable Nichuan.
An old man of the river, weary and spent, none can compare with him. What need is there to ask about his future path? He has trampled the great earth, leaving no trace;
He has struck down the void, transcending all sentiment. Let your iron ox give birth to a calf; Let the sea-swallow follow its own nature.
The Sound of Thunder: A Verse of Farewell Spoken at the Hour of Death.
To His Enlightened Master. Not like the ordinary chirping of earthworms in their burrows.
Following the original rhyme. In Commemoration of the Head Seat Huanyin, Leading the Assembly at the Dharma Assembly in Fengyang.
Expounding the Dharma at Haoliang, you occupy the foremost seat; your voice reaches the ten thousand nations, bringing joy to all faces. Four flowers swirl around the seats of humans and devas;
a hundred jewels radiantly adorn the Tiger-Panther Pass. The majestic divine talisman hangs behind your elbow;
the brilliant sword of wisdom dangles between your brows. Three thousand dragon-elephants follow your lofty steps; as the year draws to a close and the river is empty, we pray that you return soon.
To the Chan practitioner Bai:
Your pure karma is refined through the steadfastness of your ascetic practices; yet, because you have not yet clarified the ground of the mind, you apply even greater鞭策 (whips).

Outside the teachings of the Three Vehicles, there is fundamentally no dharma; before the seven-foot mat, how could there be any Chan? Do not emulate Shao-lin’s empty wall-gazing; let it be taught that Nan-yueh [Hui-ke] himself...
Grinding a tile. An iron ox snaps the golden rope; its nostrils reach toward heaven, unpierced by any hook.
Amidst the boat at Longtan, I send this to Zen Master Quanshi of Tianjie:
having been granted imperial permission to return to the mountains, I catch a favorable wind; my Wu-boat is like a house as I sail east along the Great River.

The Sage Emperor possesses the Way, surpassing even the benevolence of the ancestral temples; I, a wild monk of no talent, am ashamed to compare myself to Master Liǎn. The surging waves are all the result of Your Majesty’s sagely grace;

vast as heaven and earth, I am but a solitary wild goose in the darkness. For three years I have lived abroad on alms, having rendered no service at all; turning my head toward the Dragon River, my thoughts are boundless.
Chan Master Facheng: Transforming conditions through his travels, he repaired the Seshan Scripture Hall.

Chan Master Cheng, take care not to fall into the city of doubt. When discussing the merit of giving and receiving, one is merely obstructed by what hangs in the breast. The Great Dharma is originally without a single word;

the World-Honored One Śākyamuni spoke of the Three Vehicles as a skillful means. This treasury of radiant light illuminates heaven and mirrors earth, filling the valleys and filling the ditches with its brilliance.
A tangle of vines. Following worldly conditions with impartial transformation, the path of the practitioner is like fire burning through ice.
To the layman Wu Wuwang, he showed how to build a humble retreat beneath Fu Jin Ridge; with fire-seeds and knife-plowing, his hair has already turned white. Māmakī has a wife who is called Dharma.
Joy! The World-Honored One Śākyamuni had a son named Rāhula; in the realm of ultimate reality, there is no falsehood. Through three great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, who has advanced in cultivation?
Recognizing the original source, the mind itself is the Buddha—kicking a hundred-flower ball out from amidst the fire.
In the same rhyme, shown to the Abbot Wan-shou Yin-cang:

Fundamentally equal, there is neither distance nor intimacy. To study the Way, one must surely realize the true cause. It is only because sentient beings are deluded regarding the precious treasury That the Great Awakened One was compelled to abandon the golden wheel.
On the northern mountain, the secret transmission was the honey on the edge of the blade; At the western slope, the full raising of the eye [of wisdom].
Inner dust. Even "flint-fire and lightning-flash" is still dull. When the occasion arises, there is neither self nor person.

On the sixteenth day of the tenth month in the year of Ding-si, I mourn my Dharma brother Fangya of Kaiyuan. When the old man Kaiyuan entered *nirvāṇa*, he stepped with faith and overturned the floating Buddha.

The Hall. Having passed through the entire body at Listening-to-Autumn Pavilion, the assembly requested a verse; I have thus written this verse: "The Ultimate Way transcends words—how could there be words?
For seventy-one years, I have been without obstruction. My discourse has traveled to both the East and the West."
The old Chan master passed away at Jingxi Temple; every single thing fully manifests the pure Dharma-body. The horn-shedding mud ox plows the azure void;
the pregnant jade hare rolls through the red dust. The twin feet displayed—the form is indeed wondrous; the tune of non-arising grows ever new.
Coming and going through the gate of great tranquil concentration, the *dharma-flower* blooms once more in the spring of Shaolin.
In the same rhyme. To Zen Practitioner Ming at Huhlonghe Temple:
The assembly is as vast as a forest; If you wish to seek the profound principle, You must surely realize your own fundamental mind.

He was able to transmit the Dharma of Nanyue Huairang; Su obtained the lineage of Jingshan Zhiyin. Daily life should be lofty and pure; clouds arise from the nature-ground’s shade. Following the original rhyme:

To Venora Wen, who has realized that beyond the hearing of sounds, true emptiness is the site of enlightenment. The functional application at Longhe is distinct; the teaching at Vulture Peak is long-standing.
The gate is closed through the spring rains; the body is complete with the fivefold fragrance. Fines are paid and he leaves the monastery—do not mistake this for mere deliberation.
Presented to Attendant Min. Furthermore, a note to Du Baiyun: Your skillful application is praised as divine and swift;
your reputation has long since spread throughout the monastic forests. Yongjia felt pity for you after a single night’s stay; Xueqiao feels ashamed that you have ascended the peaks three times.
We all admire your extraordinary lineage; we look deeply to you to continue the ancestral lamp. The National Preceptor is among the guests; he calls for you—answer quickly!

You, Chan practitioner Da, have traveled through the clouds and mountains as an excellent disciple; you should realize that the objective realm is but mind. You yourself say you have traveled through the capital and personally visited Master Daolin.

The head-word is clear and vivid; yet the debt of one’s feet still presses on. Do not begrudge diligent inquiry and prostration; the Gate of Mystery is as deep as the sea. To the Chan practitioner Shouzheng:

If you can maintain rectitude while practicing Chan, then evil thoughts may fly about at will. Try to investigate the place where they fly about; in the end, they return to the time of profound stillness.
All realms are vast and resonant, not separated by so much as a hair’s breadth. To know the essential point beyond words, the void unfurls its smiling brows.

O well-established Chan practitioner, you have traveled the lands and dwell amidst banks of white clouds; having long consulted with masters and thoroughly explored the profound essence, why should you not emerge from the emerald mists?

In all directions there is no separate dharma; these words are precious for deep understanding. On the traveler’s road, one is startled by the early autumn; at every turn, they serve as a guiding compass.
*Three Poems on an Autumn Night in a Mountain Tower* The moonlight is white as day;
The shadows of the pines are as thick as clouds. The windows are empty and the mountains seem about to fall; The lamp wick sputters as the night begins to part.
The reflection of the river is seen amidst the sky; the sound of the spring is heard through the trees. Sitting alone upon this small tower, with whom can I discuss this scene?
Withered grass lines the secluded path; sparse woods emerge beyond the low wall. The wind turns, startling the birds at rest; the dew falls, making the cold cicadas weep.
Everything is vivid and without confusion; every aspect manifests itself spontaneously. Having sat cross-legged for a long time, I again burn incense in the earthen incense burner.
The mountain pavilion is fine in autumn; on my simple couch, I do not sleep at night. Moved by the season, I think of the Buddha’s fruition; reflecting on the scene, I remember Nanquan.
How lofty is the mind beneath the moon; how profound are the words in the deepening night. How vast is the intent of a thousand ages; sitting upright alone, one transcends all.

Sent to Master De-yan Xing, Lecturer on the Seven Emperors’ Discourse on the Mind by National Teacher Zhen. Sitting alone by the rain-splashed window, I contemplate your graceful bearing. You are the branch of the lineage that fulfilled the dream of the dragon-transformation.
Present: A solitary branch of the *udumbara* has been seen amidst the lush foliage.
Sent to the Record-keeper Luohan Chen Wanshi (then dwelling in mourning for his father) at Dongting.
Autumn winds stir the leaves, the waves surge upon Dongting; they bring sorrow to the Nārada of the mountains. When affection and love are exhausted, affliction [arises].
All is finished. It is good to take up my flask and staff and depart from the misty vines.
(In the same rhyme, by Wei Taipu, Hanlin Academician.
Days spent translating scriptures on the banks of the Hulu River in Qiantang; The time when I stood my horse at the head of Xizi Lake. We have spoken exhaustively of mountain clouds and the sea.
Moon. This feeling is known only to the white gulls.
Sent to the Venerable Lánshí of Púcí Dōngtáng, an eighty-year-old at Cāngxuě Tower:
empty flowers and illusory realms have all been melted away. A gentle breeze, long days; Nánshān.
At the foot of the mountain, leaning on my staff, I wade through the forest to view the bamboo shoots;
I summon Yuan to lead the repentance ceremony and appoint him as the record-keeper.

He treated him like his own son, causing him to shave his head and receive full ordination. When the Master heard that Master Xianshou was lecturing on the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*, he went to listen.
Before the chapter had even concluded, he smiled broadly and said: "The single true dharmadhātu is perfectly identical to the great void;
yet as soon as it is touched by words, it becomes a superfluous teaching. Even if the heavens were to rain down precious flowers, what benefit would they bring me?"
He then hurried to Jianye, where he visited Master Guangzhi Xin at the Great Longxiang Jiqing Temple. Guangzhi, through his literary talent and moral integrity, had moved the world;

figures such as Zhang Wenmu Gong Qiyuan, Zhang Lugu Gong Zhu, and Wei Zuocheng Su all associated with him, finding joy in exchanging verses of praise and response. When the Master slightly revealed his literary brilliance, [it was like] pearls...

The luster of his polished jade-like countenance was radiant. When Guǎngzhì and the various eminent monks saw him, they were greatly astonished; they vied with one another to recommend him, fearing only that they might be too late.
His fellow monk, the venerable Yù, scolded him, saying: "Your talent is so brilliant and spirited; why do you not contemplate bearing the great Dharma?"
"Must I become a mere slave to the poetry of the *Sāo*? What understanding can I possibly have of Master Wujindeng’s verse concerning the 'fluttering yellow leaves'?
My tongue is sealed and I cannot answer. He then returned to Haeyun, his chest as if obstructed by a massive boulder.
For over a month, his eyes did not cross at the eyelids. Suddenly, seeing autumn leaves blown down into the courtyard, he attained a sudden realization.

His functional wisdom became manifest and clear; everything he encountered was free from obstruction. Although the Master rejoiced in this, he feared that by not seeking correction from those who possessed the Way, he might fall into partiality or attachment.
Thereupon, he took up his staff and traveled to Hulin, ascending Mount Shuangjing to pay his respects to Master Jizhao Duan and present his case.
What he had realized was extremely thorough. Initially, Chijiao had expected the Master to be a vessel for the Dharma; hearing these words, he was greatly pleased and proceeded to test him.

The Master answered according to the occasion, like a hawk swooping through the autumn sky while a hare scurries across the wild plains; their spiritual resonance met with no gap wider than a single hair.
Before long, Chijiao ordered him to attend at his side to facilitate inquiries and discussions. Shortly thereafter, he was promoted to the position of *zhuchi* (abbot).
In his library, the Master took up the teachings of the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the scriptures, further warming himself to their meaning through repeated study.
His realization of the essence and his mastery of the expositions flowed forth like suspended rivers, his fame and brilliance resplendent, instantly surpassing all the elders of his time.

In the *Renwu* year of the Yuan *Zhizheng* era, the Jiangnan Branch of the Xuanzheng Yuan nominated the Master to take charge of the world at Longjiao Temple in Changguo. The people of the coastal regions and the *Qingjing*...
The fourfold assembly held incense and flowers in their hands and welcomed him from a hundred *li* with joy, as if they were beholding the Buddhas themselves.

When the Master ascended the seat to preach the Dharma, he was like a great general raising his banners and drums to issue commands; all who heard him were awestruck and submissive. On the day of Yiyou (the twenty-second day of the tenth month).
He turned his universal compassion toward neighboring lands. His vigorous encouragement and guidance were like those during the height of the formal teaching era.

In the year Wuxu, the Left Chancellor of the Jiangzhe Provincial Administration, Daśibhūmi (Daśiktemür), who concurrently held office at the Imperial Academy, invited the Master to preside over Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou.
Amidst the hardships, distress, and perils following the ravages of war, which others could not endure, the Master applied his resources with skillful means, and his exemplary conduct was most lofty.
The entire community was imbued with the lingering elegance of a peaceful era. Compared to Puci, gentlemen often remarked that he surpassed him;

even the Chancellor remarked that he had not yet fully realized the way of honoring one's teacher. In the autumn of the year Xinchou, he was again invited to serve as the abbot of Jingshan to succeed Jizhao in his former position.
The Master accepted without hesitation and departed. His reputation spread throughout the four quarters, and those who examined his virtue became ever more numerous. Even the lawless...
A man named Jufan was habitually gluttonous for meals. The head cook grew weary of him, so Jufan took his leave and went to lodge a complaint with an official of the provincial administration.
The officials of the court accepted a bribe and falsely accused the Master of colluding in a private affair. The official then arrested the Master to interrogate him on the matter.
The Master showed no sign of fear. On the *guimao* day, the two provincial administrations petitioned on his behalf regarding his innocence, compelling him to return to Mount Jing.
Monastics and laypeople alike rushed to meet him as if he were their parent; some, overcome by the intensity of their joy, even wept with grief.

When the Dragon of the Imperial Ming rose, in the *guichou* year of the Hongwu era, an imperial edict summoned more than ten Buddhist monks who possessed the Way to assemble at the Great Tianjie Monastery in the capital;
the Master was indeed at their head. Due to illness, he was unable to attend the imperial audience.

In the *yimao* year, he was granted leave to return to Qionglung Mountain, which is the site where Haiyun resided. In the eighth month of the *wumu* year, he suddenly manifested slight illness, until—
On the fourth day of the ninth month, he took up his brush to write a verse and passed away. On the ninth day, the rite of *caitya-vihāra* (cremation) was performed;

the flames transformed into five colors, and a fragrance like that of *agaru* (aloewood) wafted forth, permeating the air. His teeth, jawbone, and prayer beads remained unharmed, and his relics were of a deep, lustrous azure.

It was the color of a blue *vaiḍūrya* gem, with *śrīphala* fruits strung together above it. On that day, his disciples, including Da-jun and Shi-long, hid it in the shade of the mountain where they resided.
They took the precious remains of his nails and hair and returned to Jing-shan, where they selected a site to the right of the stupa of Master Wu-deng Cai and buried them there.
He lived for sixty-eight years and had been a monk for fifty-one summer retreats. He ordained his younger brother.

He had several disciples, and several among them succeeded to his Dharma. The Master’s physical presence was as majestic as a mountain; he stood tall and upright like a solitary pine rising from a ravine.
His authority was solemn and strict, such that none among his subordinates dared to disobey his commands. Consequently, wherever he went, all neglected undertakings were fully restored.

However, in managing affairs and responding to changing circumstances, as well as in guiding and introducing those who followed him, he was like the spring breeze and timely rain reaching all things, causing people to remain unaware of his influence.
Emperor Yuan regarded him as a worthy man and bestowed upon him this current title.

While the Master resided at Tianjie Monastery, I, Lian, had the opportunity to hear some of his introductory discourses. Upon his passing, his senior disciple Puqing, the abbot Daoyan, [recorded these teachings].
For this reason, he has described his own conduct and requested an inscription. Now, the perfectly luminous and wondrous nature truly encompasses the three thousand realms;

the four types of noble beings and the six classes of ordinary beings all manifest from within it. The Buddhas, having no choice but to do so, preached the sutras, which stirred like thunder and awakened those in hibernation.
The saying that "the wind blows and the grass bends" is intended to clarify this very nature.

That the various patriarchs, driven by necessity, set aside the scriptures and severed their branches and leaves to directly explore the fundamental root was likewise to clarify this nature. Where this nature resides, there the Way resides.
Alas, the Way has been lost and human nature has gone astray. This is not true only of the students;

even those who serve as teachers and models for the age devote themselves entirely to the trivialities of minor studies and artistic crafts to provide themselves with refined diversions. Their departure from the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is indeed vast.
If there is such a teacher as this, how can we fail to honor him as a model and mirror for the southeastern region? The Teacher emerged...
During his time in the world, the rocks of Mount Qionglong moved at night; upon his arrival at Puci, a deity descended among men and described the Master’s appearance as pure and austere.
That Heaven brought forth this Master was surely no mere coincidence. There are recorded transcripts of his four assemblies;
since their essential points have already been fully set down there, I dare not repeat them here. The inscription reads:
The various patriarchs of both China and India realized that all is but mind. Encompassing heaven and earth, they open the yang and close the yin;
the myriad phenomena, teeming and vast, are all contained within this totality. How could one be willing to discard the entire body to be confined by a single hair?
For generations their lineage has continued, their path never diverging; they harmonize the small and the great, free from obstruction and constraint.
How admirable is the Zen Master! His spiritual vision rises solitary and lofty; his literary brilliance gradually shines forth.

Like flowing clouds or surging mountains, he suddenly shifts his resolve to face the wall in self-cultivation. Gathering his thoughts to enter meditative absorption, it is as if cutting through tangled silk.
As autumn leaves fall, they drift down onto the courtyard tiles. Looking up at the blue sky, it is a single expanse of azure stretching ten thousand miles.
Awakening to the nature of self, he realized the teachings of the great masters; their sharp wits met in collision like clashing swords and halberds.
Emerging from the shores of the ocean of worldly existence, gods and humans joined their palms in reverence. Auspicious signs were manifested with omens of grace:
white stones ran about at night as he fully wielded the Seal of Orthodoxy. The Dharma drum was struck repeatedly; those who heard with their eyes severed the empty flowers of delusion.
Because his vision was steadfast, he transformed consciousness into wisdom; pearls and gems fell upon his paper.
The high ministers of the various provinces dispatched envoys to welcome him as he ascended Nanping. It is the fragrance of virtue alone that makes a mountain famous;
among the five renowned peaks, Shuangjing stands first. This is not out of partiality toward my Master, but because it serves as a mirror for the lands of the southeast.
The frivolous and petty fellows, alas, do not chastise themselves; How can one worry about blueflies before a brilliant white jade?
With winds surging and waves tossing, ten thousand words of lamentation and pity arise; But when right and wrong are made clear, he returns once more to his former seat.
When the Master departed, the springs and streams wept; Now that the Master returns, the plants and trees harbor their splendor.
His worldly conditions having ended, he passed away with a smile; his relics, like pearls, were set within his dark-blue bones.
Those of inferior learning vied to gather them, while his refined arts were widely bestowed. Why not look back upon yourself? The fundamental reality resides right here.
The radiance left behind has shone for a thousand years and yet remains but shallow. Behold it and revere it—who would dare not exert themselves?
